terminal-filesystem-model.proof: A script that creates a directory tree, walks into it with a relative path, and prints its resolved absolute working directory + a sorted listing.
terminal-filesystem-model.unlock: You can predict where a relative path resolves from any working directory, and read an absolute path as a route from /.
terminal-filesystem-model.outcome: Reason about the shell as a program with a current working directory, and move around a real tree with absolute vs relative paths, . and .. and ~.
terminal-filesystem-model.doNotClaim: Don't claim you 'know the terminal' because commands run — you know it when you can predict what a relative path resolves to before you press Enter.

terminal-filesystem-model.text: A deploy script fails with "file not found" on the CI box but works on your laptop. The script used a relative path like data/seed.sql, and CI ran it from a different working directory. The bug is not the file — it is that a relative path means nothing without knowing the current working directory. This lesson makes that model explicit so path bugs die at design time.

Every shell command runs inside a process that has ONE piece of hidden state: its current working directory (cwd). ls, cat, git, node — all resolve relative paths against that cwd. The filesystem is a single tree rooted at /. An absolute path (starts with /) is a full route from the root; a relative path (data/seed.sql, ../logs) is resolved from wherever you currently are. Get this and "file not found" becomes a solvable question: what was the cwd?

terminal-filesystem-model.prompt: Before reading: your cwd is /home/dev/app. You run `cat ../config/db.env`. Which absolute file does the shell actually open?
terminal-filesystem-model.reveal: /home/dev/config/db.env. The `..` climbs one level from /home/dev/app to /home/dev, then config/db.env descends from there. Relative paths are always resolved against the cwd, and `..` is the parent directory — so the same command opens different files depending on where you run it.

terminal-filesystem-model.code:
mkdir -p project/src project/docs   # -p makes parents, no error if they exist
cd project/src                       # relative move: cwd is now .../project/src
pwd                                  # prints the ABSOLUTE current working directory
cd ../docs                           # .. climbs to project, then into docs
ls ..                                # list the PARENT of cwd (project): docs, src
terminal-filesystem-model.intro: Build a small tree, move with a relative path, and prove where you landed with pwd (the absolute cwd).
steps: mkdir -p makes the whole path, creating parents and staying silent if they already exist.
cd changes the ONE hidden state — the cwd — and every later relative path resolves from there.
pwd prints the absolute path of the cwd; it is the ground truth when a relative path surprises you.
.. is the parent directory and . is the cwd itself; ~ expands to your home directory.
terminal-filesystem-model.commonMistake: Assuming a relative path is relative to the SCRIPT file. It is not — it is relative to the process cwd at run time, which is why the same script breaks when CI invokes it from a different directory.

terminal-filesystem-model.text: A shell is just a running process, and it carries one crucial piece of state: the current working directory. When you type `cat notes.txt`, the shell silently resolves that relative name against the cwd, so it really opens <cwd>/notes.txt. The filesystem itself is a single tree with root /. A path that starts with / is ABSOLUTE — a complete route the shell follows from the root, identical no matter where you are. Any other path is RELATIVE and is joined onto the cwd. Three special names do the heavy lifting: `.` is the cwd, `..` is its parent (climb up one level), and `~` expands to your home directory. `cd` is the only command that changes the cwd; `pwd` prints it. Because the cwd is invisible in the command text, most "file not found" bugs are really "wrong cwd" bugs — the fix is to make the path absolute or to set the cwd deliberately before you run.
terminal-filesystem-model.title: The cwd is the shell's hidden argument to every command

navigate-inspect-files.proof: A script that counts lines in a generated file and prints its first N lines, computing both from the file rather than echoing them.
navigate-inspect-files.unlock: You can answer "what is in this directory and this file" from the shell in under five seconds.
navigate-inspect-files.outcome: Inspect a directory and files without opening an editor: ls -la to see hidden files + permissions, wc/head/tail to sample content, and file to identify type.
navigate-inspect-files.doNotClaim: Don't claim you inspected a file because you cat-ed it — a 2GB log needs head/tail/less, and cat would flood your terminal or hang it.

navigate-inspect-files.text: You SSH into a server to debug a failing job. You cannot open an IDE. You need to know: what files are here (including the dotfiles), how big is the log, and what do its last 20 lines say. Reaching for cat on a giant log freezes the session. This lesson gives you the surgical inspection tools that scale from a 3-line config to a multi-gigabyte log.

Reading before writing is most of real debugging. ls lists a directory (-l long form with permissions/size, -a includes dotfiles like .gitignore and .env, -1 one per line for scripting). For file content you rarely want the whole thing: head -n shows the top, tail -n the bottom (tail -f follows a growing log live), wc -l counts lines, and less pages interactively. file names the type by content, not extension. These are the eyes you use before you touch anything.

navigate-inspect-files.prompt: Before reading: you need the LAST 50 lines of a 4GB app.log on a remote box with a slow link. What do you run, and what do you NOT run?
navigate-inspect-files.reveal: Run `tail -n 50 app.log` — it seeks to the end and reads only the tail, cheap even on a 4GB file. Do NOT run `cat app.log` (streams all 4GB over the slow link and floods your terminal) and do not open it in an editor that loads the whole file into memory. tail -f app.log would then stream new lines live.

navigate-inspect-files.code:
ls -la                 # long listing WITH dotfiles: perms, size, name (.env shows up)
wc -l app.log          # how many lines total — decide before you read
head -n 20 app.log     # the first 20 lines (the boot banner / header)
tail -n 20 app.log     # the last 20 lines (the most recent events)
file logo.png          # identify by content: "PNG image data", not by the name
navigate-inspect-files.intro: List a directory including dotfiles, then sample a file three ways instead of dumping it.
steps: ls -la reveals hidden dotfiles (.gitignore, .env) and each file's permission bits and size.
wc -l tells you the scale first, so you never blindly cat a huge file.
head/tail read only one end of the file — constant cost regardless of size.
file inspects the bytes to report the real type, so a mislabeled .txt that is really a zip is caught.
navigate-inspect-files.commonMistake: Using plain `ls` and concluding a directory has no config, when the config is a dotfile (.gitignore, .env, .github) that only `ls -a` reveals. Half of a repo's important files start with a dot.

navigate-inspect-files.text: Inspection tools differ by WHERE and HOW MUCH they read. ls reads directory entries: -l gives the long form (permission string, owner, byte size, name), -a adds entries starting with a dot (which the shell hides by default — that is the ONLY thing "hidden" means here), and -1 prints one name per line for piping. For file content, the key insight is that you almost never want all of it: head -n K reads the first K lines and stops; tail -n K seeks near the end and reads the last K — both are cheap on a huge file because they do not read the middle. tail -f keeps the file open and prints new lines as they are appended, which is how you watch a live log. wc -l counts lines (wc -c counts bytes). less pages through interactively without loading everything into memory. file reads the leading "magic" bytes to identify the type from content, not the extension. The discipline: check the size (wc), then read the end you care about (head/tail), and only page (less) or dump (cat) when the file is genuinely small.
navigate-inspect-files.title: Sample files by the end you need, never dump them whole
Choosing an inspection tool by size and target
navigate-inspect-files.subtitle: small file vs huge log, top vs bottom

storyboard.say: You are SSH'd into a server with no IDE, and you need to read a file safely — everything starts from that need.
The first question is not what to open but how big it is — file size decides which tool is safe to reach for.
If the file is small, just dump it: cat prints it all, or less pages through it interactively.
But on a huge log, cat freezes your session — so the huge branch forks to a different question entirely.
For a big file the real choice is which end you care about: the top or the tail.
Want the header or start? head -n K reads the first K lines and stops — cheap even on gigabytes.
Want recent events? tail -n K seeks near the end, and tail -f follows new lines as the log grows live.
The core insight: inspection tools differ by where and how much they read — never read the whole giant middle.

optionA.text: Opens interactively: scroll, search with /, quit with q, and it never loads the whole file into memory. Good for anything you might scroll.
optionA.label: less (pager)

optionB.text: Dumps everything to the terminal at once. Fine for a 10-line file; for a big one it scrolls past and you cannot search.
optionB.label: cat

navigate-inspect-files.guidance: Use less for anything you might scroll or search; use cat only for genuinely tiny files or when you are piping the content into another command. The tell is: if you want to move around inside the file, you want a pager, not a dump.
navigate-inspect-files.question: To view a large config you are about to edit, cat it or open it in less?

options: The win is caching: tail holds the file in memory after the first read, so on this run it skips the disk cat still hits.
cat is faster here because it reads lazily and never buffers, while tail must load the whole file to find its final lines.
tail seeks toward the end and reads only the last lines it needs, while cat streams the entire 10GB through the pipe first.
They finish equally fast — a pipe streams data lazily, so pushing 10GB through cat adds no real cost.
navigate-inspect-files.question: Why does `tail -n 50 big.log` stay fast on a 10GB file while `cat big.log | tail -n 50` is slow?
navigate-inspect-files.explanation: tail reads from near the end of the file directly. Piping cat into tail forces cat to read and push all 10GB through the pipe before tail can take the last 50 lines — same result, wildly different cost.

items: You reveal dotfiles with ls -a instead of missing half the repo.
You check size with wc before reading a file you do not know.
You use head/tail on large files and reserve cat for small ones.

prompts: Explain why ls -a matters in a git repo specifically.

navigate-inspect-files.text: git has its own inspection verbs built on this instinct — git log is "tail for history", git show is "cat for a commit", and git diff is "read before you touch". The habit of looking before editing is what Module 2 turns into git status.

criteria: Observable evidence — You list dotfiles and permissions with ls -la
You measure before reading with wc
You sample huge files with head/tail, not cat

pipes-redirects-grep-find.proof: A pipeline that generates lines, filters them with grep, counts the matches, and writes the count to a file — the count computed by the pipeline.
pipes-redirects-grep-find.unlock: You can build a filter → transform → count pipeline and separate what goes to stdout vs stderr vs a file.
pipes-redirects-grep-find.outcome: Compose small tools with pipes and redirects, filter text with grep, and locate files with find — turning several commands into one deterministic pipeline.
pipes-redirects-grep-find.doNotClaim: Don't claim you can 'use grep' if you only match fixed strings — you own it when you filter, invert (-v), count (-c), and combine it in a pipe.

pipes-redirects-grep-find.text: A log has 40,000 lines and you need one number: how many requests returned a 500 in the last hour. Scrolling is hopeless. The Unix answer is a pipeline — grep to keep the 500 lines, wc -l to count them — one line that gives one number. This lesson teaches the composition model that makes the shell a data tool, not just a launcher.

Unix philosophy: small programs that each do one thing, connected by pipes. A pipe (|) wires one command's stdout into the next command's stdin, so `A | B | C` streams data through a filter chain. Redirects send streams to files: > overwrites, >> appends, 2> captures stderr separately, and < feeds a file as stdin. grep filters lines by pattern (-i ignore case, -v invert, -c count, -n line numbers, -r recurse). find locates files by name/type across a tree. Together they answer questions no single command can.

pipes-redirects-grep-find.prompt: Before reading: what is the difference between `cmd > out.txt 2>&1` and `cmd 2> err.txt`? Where does each stream end up?
pipes-redirects-grep-find.reveal: `cmd > out.txt 2>&1` sends stdout to out.txt AND redirects stderr to wherever stdout now points (out.txt), so both streams land in out.txt. `cmd 2> err.txt` sends ONLY stderr to err.txt while stdout still goes to the terminal. stdout (fd 1) and stderr (fd 2) are separate channels; you route them independently.

pipes-redirects-grep-find.code:
grep "ERROR" app.log | wc -l          # count only the ERROR lines (filter → count)
grep -v "DEBUG" app.log > clean.log   # keep everything EXCEPT debug, write to a file
find . -name "*.test.js" -type f      # every test file anywhere under the cwd
build 2> errors.txt                    # send only stderr to a file; stdout stays visible
pipes-redirects-grep-find.intro: Filter a stream with grep, count the survivors, and split normal output from errors.
steps: A pipe connects stdout of the left command to stdin of the right — data flows left to right.
grep keeps matching lines; -v inverts to keep NON-matching lines.
> writes (overwriting) to a file; 2> captures the separate stderr channel.
find walks a directory tree and filters by -name and -type, printing paths you can pipe onward.
pipes-redirects-grep-find.commonMistake: Using > when you meant >> and silently truncating a file you wanted to append to. `echo x > log` replaces the whole file every run; `echo x >> log` adds a line. One extra character is the difference between "append" and "destroy".

pipes-redirects-grep-find.text: Every process has three standard streams: stdin (fd 0, input), stdout (fd 1, normal output), and stderr (fd 2, errors and diagnostics). A PIPE `A | B` connects A's stdout to B's stdin, so data streams through — this is why `grep ERROR log | wc -l` works: grep emits matching lines, wc counts them, and nothing touches disk. REDIRECTS point a stream at a file instead of the terminal: `> file` sends stdout (truncating the file first), `>> file` appends, `2> file` sends stderr, `2>&1` merges stderr into wherever stdout currently goes, and `< file` feeds a file in as stdin. Keeping stdout and stderr separate is what lets you capture a program's errors without polluting its real output. grep is the workhorse filter (patterns, -v to invert, -c to count, -r to recurse, -i to ignore case), and find is the file locator (walk the tree, match by -name/-type). The whole model is composition: instead of one big tool, you chain sharp small ones, and each pipe is a place you can insert another filter.
pipes-redirects-grep-find.title: Pipes stream stdout→stdin; redirects route the three standard streams
A filter pipeline and its stream routing
pipes-redirects-grep-find.subtitle: stdout flows through pipes; stderr and files are separate

storyboard.say: You have a 40,000-line log and need one number: how many requests returned a 500. Scrolling is hopeless, so we build a pipeline.
The file feeds in as stdin. grep reads it line by line, keeping only the lines that match your error pattern.
The pipe is the key move: it wires grep's stdout straight into wc's stdin, so matching lines stream through with nothing touching disk.
wc -l counts those piped lines and writes the total to its own stdout, which lands on your terminal as one clean number.
Meanwhile grep's diagnostics ride a separate stream, stderr, so a 2> redirect can capture them to errors.txt without polluting the count.
That's the composition model: small tools joined by stdout-to-stdin pipes, with stderr kept apart so real output stays clean.

pipes-redirects-grep-find.title: Build a filter-and-count pipeline
pipes-redirects-grep-find.starter:
# Make a log where every 4th line is an ERROR, the rest INFO.
for i in $(seq 1 20); do
  if [ $((i % 4)) -eq 0 ]; then echo "line $i ERROR"; else echo "line $i INFO"; fi
done > app.log
# TODO: count ERROR lines with grep -c, write the count to errors.count,
# then print it:
#   grep -c ERROR app.log > errors.count
#   echo "error lines: $(cat errors.count)"
#   echo "total lines: $(wc -l < app.log | tr -d ' ')"
pipes-redirects-grep-find.summary: Generate 20 lines tagged INFO/ERROR, then use grep + wc to count just the ERROR lines and redirect that count into a file. The number is computed by the pipeline and read back from the file.

pipes-redirects-grep-find.fix:
# want the count on screen AND the list saved? use tee:
find . -name "*.tmp" 2>/dev/null | tee results.txt | wc -l
# tee writes stdin to the file AND passes it down the pipe
pipes-redirects-grep-find.task: stdout was redirected to a file BEFORE the pipe, so nothing reaches wc and results are split confusingly. Decide on one destination.
pipes-redirects-grep-find.symptom: A pipeline meant to save matches to a file leaves the file empty, yet errors still scroll past on screen.

optionA.text: cmd | tee out.txt streams stdout to the file AND to the terminal in one pass. One command, one read of the data.
optionA.label: tee

optionB.text: Run once to screen, once with > out.txt. Simple to think about, but you execute the command twice — wasteful and wrong if it has side effects or nondeterministic output.
optionB.label: Run it twice

pipes-redirects-grep-find.guidance: Use tee (A). Running a command twice doubles the cost and, worse, can produce two DIFFERENT outputs (timestamps, network) — so the saved file would not match what you saw. tee guarantees the file and the screen show the exact same bytes.
pipes-redirects-grep-find.question: You need to both save a command's output to a file and see it on screen. Redirect twice or use tee?

options: Each line that does NOT contain INFO, printed in full — reading -v as invert but treating -c as a "clean output" flag.
The count of lines that DO contain INFO — counting matches with -c but forgetting that -v flips which lines count.
An error, because -c reports a count while -v inverts the match, and grep refuses to combine a counter with inversion.
The COUNT of lines that do NOT contain INFO — -v inverts the match and -c reports how many lines matched.
pipes-redirects-grep-find.question: What does `grep -c -v INFO app.log` print?
pipes-redirects-grep-find.explanation: -v inverts the match (keep lines WITHOUT INFO) and -c prints the count instead of the lines. Combined, it counts every non-INFO line. Flags compose: -v changes what matches, -c changes what is printed.

items: You chain filter → transform → count with pipes instead of intermediate files.
You route stdout, stderr, and files independently (>, >>, 2>, 2>&1).
You use grep -v/-c and find -name/-type to answer questions in one line.

prompts: Explain what a pipe connects and in which direction data flows.
Explain the difference between > and >> and why it bites people.

pipes-redirects-grep-find.text: git leans on this constantly: `git log --oneline | grep fix | wc -l` counts your fix commits, and `git status --porcelain | grep "^??"` lists untracked files. Every git command that prints lines becomes composable the moment you can pipe.

criteria: Observable evidence — You build a working filter/count pipeline
You route stderr separately from stdout
You use grep -v/-c and find correctly

permissions-processes.proof: A script that creates a file, sets an exact permission mode, and prints back the resulting symbolic permission string computed by the filesystem.
permissions-processes.unlock: You can translate between symbolic (rwxr-xr-x) and octal (755) permissions and know why a script needs the x bit to run.
permissions-processes.outcome: Read and change Unix permission bits (rwx for user/group/other), make a script executable, and inspect/terminate processes with ps and kill.
permissions-processes.doNotClaim: Don't claim you understand permissions from `chmod 777` — that is a security smell, not a fix; you own it when you grant the minimum bits a task needs.

permissions-processes.text: You wrote deploy.sh and get "Permission denied" when you run ./deploy.sh, even though you can read the file fine. The problem is the execute bit is not set — reading a file and running it are different permissions. Meanwhile a runaway process is pinning a CPU and you need to find and stop it. This lesson makes the permission model and process control concrete.

Every file carries permission bits for three classes — user (owner), group, other — each with read (r=4), write (w=2), execute (x=1). ls -l shows them as a symbolic string like -rwxr-xr-x; chmod sets them symbolically (chmod +x file) or in octal (chmod 755 file). A directory's x bit means "may enter/traverse", not "run". Processes are running programs with a PID; ps lists them, kill <pid> sends a signal (default TERM, polite; kill -9 is SIGKILL, forced). This is the layer where "denied" and "stuck" live.

permissions-processes.prompt: Before reading: `chmod 640 secret.txt` sets what permissions for user, group, and other?
permissions-processes.reveal: 6=rw- for the user (read+write), 4=r-- for the group (read only), 0=--- for other (nothing). So the owner can read and write, the group can only read, and everyone else has no access. Each octal digit is the sum r(4)+w(2)+x(1) for one class, in the order user, group, other.

permissions-processes.code:
ls -l deploy.sh          # -rw-r--r-- : owner rw, group r, other r — NOT executable
chmod +x deploy.sh       # add the execute bit for all classes
ls -l deploy.sh          # -rwxr-xr-x now: the x bits are set
chmod 600 secret.env     # exact octal: owner rw, group/other nothing (rw-------)
ps aux | grep node       # find running node processes and their PIDs
kill 4823                # send SIGTERM to PID 4823 (asks it to shut down cleanly)
permissions-processes.intro: Read a permission string, add the execute bit to make a script runnable, and set an exact octal mode.
steps: ls -l's first field is the permission string: type + three rwx triplets (user, group, other).
A script needs the x (execute) bit or ./script.sh fails with Permission denied even if readable.
chmod +x adds execute; chmod NNN sets an exact octal mode where each digit sums r=4,w=2,x=1.
ps lists processes with PIDs; kill sends SIGTERM by default, kill -9 sends the unblockable SIGKILL.
permissions-processes.commonMistake: Reaching for chmod 777 to "fix" a permission error. That grants write+execute to everyone on the system — a real security hole. The fix is almost always the minimum bit that was missing (often +x on a script, or the owner not matching).

permissions-processes.text: A Unix permission is nine bits shown as three triplets: user (owner), group, other, each carrying read (r=4), write (w=2), execute (x=1). ls -l renders them symbolically — -rwxr-xr-x means owner rwx, group r-x, other r-x — and the same value in octal is 755 (7=4+2+1, 5=4+0+1). For a regular FILE, x means "may be run as a program"; for a DIRECTORY, x means "may be traversed/entered" and r means "may list its names" — a subtle but important difference. chmod changes the bits either symbolically (chmod u+x, chmod go-w) or by octal mode (chmod 640). The principle is least privilege: grant the smallest set that works, which is why 600 for a secret and 755 for a shared script are common and 777 is a red flag. PROCESSES are running programs, each with a numeric PID; ps aux lists them, and kill sends a SIGNAL to one: the default SIGTERM (15) asks it to clean up and exit, while SIGKILL (kill -9) forcibly terminates it with no chance to clean up — so you try TERM first and escalate to -9 only when it hangs.
permissions-processes.title: Permissions are three rwx triplets; processes are PIDs you signal
Permission bits and the run decision
permissions-processes.subtitle: why ./script.sh needs the execute bit

storyboard.say: You typed ./deploy.sh to run your script — the shell attempts to launch the file as a program.
To decide, the kernel reads the file's permission bits — the rwx flags stored in its mode.
The real question is narrow: does this file carry the execute bit? Reading and running are different permissions.
No x bit set — so even though you can read the file fine, the kernel refuses to run it: Permission denied.
The fix is chmod +x, which flips the missing execute bit on without touching your read or write access.
chmod rewrites the file's mode bits — the rwx string in ls -l now shows the x you added.
Now the check passes: the file has x, so the shell launches it and it runs as a live process with a PID.

permissions-processes.title: Set an exact mode and read it back

optionA.text: kill <pid> (SIGTERM) first so the process can flush buffers, close files, and release locks; only kill -9 if it refuses to die after a grace period.
optionA.label: SIGTERM, then -9 if needed

optionB.text: SIGKILL ends it instantly. Fast, but the process gets NO chance to clean up — half-written files, orphaned locks, corrupted state.
optionB.label: kill -9 immediately

permissions-processes.guidance: Default to A. SIGTERM is catchable, so well-behaved programs shut down cleanly and consistently. Reserve kill -9 (B) for a process that is truly wedged and ignoring TERM — it is a last resort precisely because it skips all cleanup.

options: Nothing at all, because for directories only the owner rwx bits are honored and the group r-x block is ignored.
Read and write files inside it, since a group r bit grants full read-and-write access to a directory and its contents.
Delete or rename files in it, reading the execute bit on a directory as permission to modify what it holds.
List the names in it and cd into it (traverse), but not create, rename, or delete entries — the group has r-x, not w.
permissions-processes.question: ls -l shows `drwxr-x---` on a directory. What can a member of the group do?
permissions-processes.explanation: The group triplet is r-x: r lets them LIST the directory's entries and x lets them ENTER/traverse it, but with no w they cannot create, rename, or delete files inside. On directories, r and x mean list and traverse — not the file meanings of read and run.

git-object-model.proof: A repo where you commit a file and then print the object TYPE of the commit, its tree, and the file blob — types computed by git cat-file.
git-object-model.unlock: You can trace a commit → its tree → the file blobs, and explain why identical content has one identical hash.
git-object-model.outcome: Explain git as a content-addressable store of four object types — blob, tree, commit, tag — and prove it by hashing content and reading object types back with cat-file.
git-object-model.doNotClaim: Don't claim git 'stores diffs' — it stores whole-content SNAPSHOTS as objects; the diff view is computed on demand.

git-object-model.text: A teammate insists "git saves the changes between versions." Then you both stare at a repo where reverting feels like magic and lost commits reappear from nowhere. The confusion is a wrong mental model. Git is not a diff pile — it is a content-addressable object database of snapshots. This lesson makes you SEE the objects, so the rest of git stops being magic.

Under .git/objects, git stores four kinds of immutable objects, each named by the hash of its own content (SHA-1 by default, SHA-256 opt-in). A BLOB is a file's bytes (no name). A TREE is a directory listing: names + modes + the blob/tree hashes they point to. A COMMIT points to one tree (the whole snapshot) plus parent commit(s) and author/message. A TAG object names a commit. Because the name IS the hash of the content, identical content is stored once, and any tampering changes the hash. Every higher-level git feature is built on these four objects.

git-object-model.prompt: Before reading: you commit the same file twice with no changes in between (touching an unrelated file each time). How many blob objects exist for that file's content — one or two?
git-object-model.reveal: One. The blob is named by the hash of its CONTENT, so identical content produces the same hash and git stores it exactly once — the second commit's tree just points at the same existing blob. This deduplication-by-content is the whole point of a content-addressable store; the commits differ, but they can share blobs and even trees.

git-object-model.code:
# A blob is just hashed content — no filename involved:
printf 'hello\n' | git hash-object --stdin      # prints the blob's SHA (of "hello\n")

# After a commit, inspect the object graph by TYPE:
git cat-file -t HEAD          # -> commit   (HEAD names the latest commit object)
git cat-file -t HEAD^{tree}   # -> tree     (the snapshot the commit points to)
git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}   # pretty-print the tree: mode, type, blob-hash, name
git-object-model.intro: Hash raw content to see a blob id, then commit and walk commit → tree → blob by type.
steps: git hash-object computes the id of content — proof that the NAME is the hash of the CONTENT.
A commit object points to exactly one tree: the complete snapshot of the project at that moment.
A tree lists entries (mode, type, hash, name); file entries point to blobs, subdirs to sub-trees.
cat-file -t shows an object's type; -p pretty-prints it — this is how you read the raw graph.
git-object-model.commonMistake: Believing a commit stores a diff from its parent. A commit stores a full tree (a complete snapshot); the "changes" you see in git show are COMPUTED by diffing that tree against the parent's tree at display time.

git-object-model.text: Git's core is astonishingly small: a key-value store where the KEY is the cryptographic hash of the VALUE. There are four object types. A BLOB holds a file's exact bytes and nothing else — no name, no path. A TREE represents a directory: a list of entries, each with a mode (e.g. 100644 normal file, 100755 executable, 040000 subdirectory), a type, the hash of the blob or sub-tree it references, and the entry's name. A COMMIT points to exactly ONE top-level tree (the full snapshot), plus zero or more PARENT commits, plus author/committer/message metadata. A TAG object gives a commit a permanent annotated name. Two consequences fall out of hashing content. First, DEDUPLICATION: identical file content is one blob no matter how many commits or paths reference it. Second, INTEGRITY: change one byte and the hash changes, cascading up through the tree to the commit — so history is tamper-evident. Git does NOT store diffs between versions; each commit is a complete snapshot, and the diffs you read are computed on the fly by comparing two trees. Default hashes are SHA-1; SHA-256 repositories are supported. Once you see git as this object graph, branches, merges, and recovery all become "which commit does this pointer point at."
git-object-model.title: Git is a content-addressable database of snapshots, not diffs
The commit → tree → blob object graph
git-object-model.subtitle: a commit is a snapshot of one tree of blobs

storyboard.say: Start where you reach into history: HEAD is just a movable ref that names one commit — a pointer, not a copy of your files.
That commit is one object holding metadata plus two links: it points backward to its parent commit, forming the history chain.
The commit's real payload is a single snapshot: it points to exactly one top-level tree capturing the whole project state.
The tree is a directory listing — each entry pairs a mode and a content hash with a name, referencing the blobs it contains.
A blob is nothing but a file's exact bytes — no name, no path; the name lives up in the tree entry, not the blob.
The key insight: every object is named by the hash of its content, so identical files dedupe and nothing stores diffs — only full snapshots.
So reverting isn't magic and lost commits reappear: HEAD just re-points to a snapshot that was always sitting in the object store.

optionA.text: Each commit = a full tree of the project. Matches how git actually stores data, so merges, resets, and recovery all make sense as "which snapshot."
optionA.label: Snapshots

optionB.text: Each commit = the diff from before. Intuitive for reading a PR, but it is a DISPLAY model, not the storage model — it breaks down the moment you reason about branches or reflog.
optionB.label: Changes/diffs

git-object-model.guidance: Teach snapshots (A) as the storage truth and treat diffs (B) as a convenient VIEW git computes for you. People who hold the diff model as reality get repeatedly surprised by resets and merges; the snapshot model predicts them.
git-object-model.question: When explaining git to a new teammate, describe commits as "snapshots" or as "changes"?

options: One tree (the whole snapshot) plus its parent commit(s) and the author, date, and message metadata.
The changed blobs directly, listing each modified file content object with no tree in between them.
The branch it lives on, so a commit stores the name of the branch whose tip currently points at it.
The diff against its parent for each changed file, since git records a commit as the set of changes it introduced.
git-object-model.question: A commit object directly references which of these?
git-object-model.explanation: A commit points to exactly one top-level tree (the full snapshot) and to its parent commit(s), with metadata. It does not store diffs (computed on demand), does not skip the tree, and knows nothing about branch names — a branch is a separate ref that points at the commit.

staging-index-commits.proof: A repo where, after staging one of two changed files, git status --porcelain shows the precise staged/unstaged split.
staging-index-commits.unlock: You can explain the three states — working tree, index, committed — and predict porcelain XY codes.
staging-index-commits.outcome: Use the index (staging area) deliberately: stage specific changes, read the two-column porcelain status, and craft a commit that contains exactly what you intend.
staging-index-commits.doNotClaim: Don't claim `git add .` is 'saving your work' — add only copies changes into the index; nothing is saved until commit, and add . may stage things you did not mean to.

staging-index-commits.text: You fixed a bug AND left a debug print in the same file, then ran git add . and git commit -am "fix". The debug line shipped. The miss is that git has a middle layer — the index — that lets you commit exactly the fix and leave the noise behind, but only if you stage deliberately. This lesson makes the index a tool you drive, not a step you skip.

Git has THREE trees you move content between: the WORKING TREE (your files on disk), the INDEX / staging area (a proposed next snapshot), and HEAD (the last commit). git add copies a change from the working tree INTO the index; git commit turns the index into a new commit. git status --porcelain prints one line per changed path with a two-character XY code: X is the index (staged) status, Y is the working-tree status. Understanding this split is what lets you build a clean, reviewable commit instead of a dump of everything you touched.

staging-index-commits.prompt: Before reading: you edit a tracked file, run git add on it, then edit it AGAIN. What does git commit capture — the first edit, the second, or both?
staging-index-commits.reveal: Only the FIRST edit — the version you staged. git add snapshots the file INTO the index at that moment; the later edit lives only in the working tree and is not staged, so the commit contains the staged version. git status would show the path with BOTH a staged change (X) and an unstaged change (Y). You would need to add again to include the second edit.

staging-index-commits.code:
git status --porcelain   #  M app.js   (space-M: modified in working tree, not staged)
                         # ?? notes.txt (untracked)
git add app.js           # copy app.js's change into the index
git status --porcelain   # M  app.js   (M-space: staged) ... note the COLUMN shifted left
git commit -m "fix"      # turn the staged index into a commit; notes.txt stays untracked
staging-index-commits.intro: Stage one file, leave another unstaged, and read the porcelain codes that describe the split.
steps: The first porcelain column (X) is the index; the second (Y) is the working tree.
M (space then M) means modified but NOT staged; M  (M then space) means staged.
?? means untracked — git is not tracking that path at all yet.
commit packages the INDEX into a snapshot; whatever is only in the working tree is left out.
staging-index-commits.commonMistake: Treating git add . and git commit -am as one atomic "save". add . stages every change in the tree (including stray files and debug edits), and -am only auto-stages already-TRACKED files — new files still get missed while junk gets included. Stage deliberately and read status before committing.

staging-index-commits.text: Between your files on disk and the committed history sits a third thing most people skip: the INDEX (also called the staging area or cache). It is a proposed next snapshot. Content moves through three states. WORKING TREE — the actual files you edit. INDEX — what will go into the next commit, populated by git add. HEAD — the most recent commit. git add copies a path's current content from the working tree into the index; git commit writes the index out as a new commit object and advances the branch. This is why the index matters: it lets you commit a SUBSET — stage the bug fix, leave the debug line unstaged, and the commit is clean. git status --porcelain is the machine-readable X/Y view: X is the path's status in the index (staged), Y is its status in the working tree. Common codes: "M " staged-modified, " M" unstaged-modified, "MM" staged then further edited, "A " newly added/staged, "??" untracked, " D" deleted-in-tree. Because add SNAPSHOTS content at the moment you run it, editing after staging leaves the new edit unstaged — the index holds the version you added, not the file's latest bytes. Driving the index deliberately is the difference between a curated history and a pile of "wip" commits.
staging-index-commits.title: The index is a staging snapshot between disk and history
The three trees and the commands that move content
staging-index-commits.subtitle: working tree → index → commit

storyboard.say: Start on disk: the working tree holds the files you actually edit — here, your bug fix and a stray debug print sit side by side.
git add copies a change out of the working tree and into the index — the staging area that will become your next commit.
The index is the layer most people skip: a proposed next snapshot you assemble deliberately, not a mirror of your whole disk.
git commit turns whatever is in the index into a new commit object, and HEAD advances to point at it.
git status --porcelain prints one XY line per path: X reads the index, Y reads the working tree — the two columns are two different trees.
That X/Y split is the risk: staged and unstaged are separate states, so 'git add .' sweeps the debug line in alongside your fix.
The insight: stage a subset — add only the fix, leave the debug line unstaged, and commit exactly what you mean to ship.

It was modified twice and both of those edits are staged, so the two M columns count the two changes now in the index.
It is untracked — the two M columns mark a brand-new file git has never recorded and is now reporting twice.

reading-history.proof: A repo with three commits where you print the commit count and the exact subject lines with git log --oneline formatting.
reading-history.unlock: You can answer "when and why did this line change" by combining log, diff, and blame.
reading-history.outcome: Read a repository's past: shape git log output, diff any two points (working tree, index, commits), and use blame to find the commit behind a line.
reading-history.doNotClaim: Don't claim you 'checked the history' by scrolling git log — you own it when you can diff a specific range and blame a specific line.

reading-history.text: A config value is wrong in production and nobody remembers changing it. "Who set timeout to 3 and when?" is answerable in seconds — git blame points at the exact commit, git show explains why, git log --oneline gives the shape. Without these you guess; with them you have receipts. This lesson turns history from a wall of text into a query tool.

Three verbs read the past. git log lists commits reachable from a start point (default HEAD), newest first; formatting flags like --oneline, --graph, and -n K shape and bound it. git diff shows changes BETWEEN two of git's trees: no args = working tree vs index, --cached = index vs HEAD, and A..B = between two commits. git blame annotates every line of a file with the commit, author, and date that last touched it. Reachability matters: log shows history behind a ref, so it naturally follows parents back through the object graph you learned in the object-model lesson.

reading-history.prompt: Before reading: what is the difference between `git diff`, `git diff --cached`, and `git diff HEAD`?
reading-history.reveal: git diff (no args) = working tree vs the INDEX (your unstaged changes). git diff --cached (or --staged) = the INDEX vs HEAD (what you have staged, i.e. what a commit would include). git diff HEAD = working tree vs HEAD (ALL changes, staged and unstaged, since the last commit). Each picks a different pair of git's three trees to compare.

reading-history.code:
git log --oneline -n 5        # compact: short-hash + subject, newest 5 commits
git log --oneline --graph     # ASCII branch/merge topology alongside the subjects
git diff --cached             # exactly what is staged (index vs HEAD) — pre-commit review
git show HEAD                 # the full patch + metadata of the latest commit
git blame config.yml          # per-line: which commit/author last changed each line
reading-history.intro: Shape log output, then diff the staged change and blame a line.
steps: git log walks parents back from HEAD; --oneline compresses each commit to hash + subject.
--graph draws the branch/merge topology so you can see where history forked and joined.
git diff picks two of the three trees; --cached compares the index to HEAD (your staged set).
git blame maps each line to the commit that last modified it — the entry point to "why".
reading-history.commonMistake: Reading git log to answer "who changed THIS line" — log shows commits, not line ownership, so you end up scrolling. blame answers line-level "who/when" directly, and git log -L traces a line range over time.

reading-history.text: Reading history is three distinct questions, each with its own tool. WHAT is the shape of the past? git log walks the commit graph backward from a starting ref (HEAD by default), following parent pointers, printing newest-first. It is not a flat file — it is a traversal of reachable commits, which is why --graph can render forks and merges and why `git log branchA..branchB` shows commits on B not on A. WHAT changed between two points? git diff always compares exactly TWO of git's trees: with no args, working tree vs index (unstaged edits); --cached, index vs HEAD (staged edits); HEAD, working tree vs HEAD (everything since the last commit); and A..B or A B, one commit against another. Naming the two sides is the whole skill. WHO last touched a line and WHEN? git blame annotates each line of a file with the commit, author, and timestamp that last changed it — the launchpad for "why did this become 3?", which you then answer with git show <that-commit> to read the full patch and message. The reachability idea from the object model is the connective tissue: log follows parents, diff compares snapshots, blame resolves a line to the snapshot that introduced it. Together they turn a repo into a queryable record instead of a scroll.
reading-history.title: log walks reachable commits, diff compares two trees, blame maps lines to commits

storyboard.say: A config value is wrong in production and nobody remembers changing it. Everything you need lives here, in the commit history.
Reading the past is three distinct questions, and the commit store answers each one with its own tool.
First question: what is the shape? git log walks the graph backward from HEAD, printing commits newest-first.
Second question: what changed? git diff compares exactly two of git's trees, like commit A against commit B.
Third question: who set this line? git blame annotates every line of the file with the commit that last touched it.
Blame hands you the guilty commit, so git show opens that exact commit to explain why the change was made.
Log works the same way: scan the shape, pick a commit, then git show reads its full story. Now you have receipts, not guesses.

branches.text: A teammate avoids branches because "making a copy of the whole project per feature is heavy." That belief makes them pile unrelated work onto main and fear experiments. The reality flips it: a branch is a tiny pointer, branching is free, and it is the safest way to try something. This lesson makes branches concrete so you branch fearlessly.

A branch is not a folder or a copy — it is a lightweight, MOVABLE reference: a small file under .git/refs/heads/ containing the hash of ONE commit. HEAD is a special pointer that usually points at a branch ref, marking "the branch you are currently on"; committing advances the current branch ref forward and drags HEAD along. Because a branch is just a pointer, creating one is instant and cheap, and multiple branches can point into the same shared commit graph, diverging only where they add different commits.

branches.prompt: Before reading: you have main at commit C3. You run `git switch -c feature` and immediately `git commit`. Where do main and feature point now?
branches.reveal: main still points at C3 (untouched). feature was created pointing at C3, and your new commit C4 advanced feature to C4 while HEAD followed feature. So main=C3, feature=C4, and C4's parent is C3 — the branches share all history up to C3 and diverge at the new commit. Creating the branch copied nothing; it just added a second pointer to C3.

git switch -c feature     # create 'feature' pointing at the current commit, and switch to it

echo "x" >> app.js
git add app.js && git commit -m "feature work"   # advances 'feature' + HEAD, NOT main
git branch -v             # list branches, each with the short hash it points at
git switch main           # HEAD now points at main again; working tree matches main

branches.commonMistake: Thinking you must "save" or copy files before switching branches. Switching updates the working tree to the target branch's snapshot automatically — but uncommitted changes can block or follow the switch, which is exactly why stash (Module 4) exists.

branches.text: Three things people conflate are actually distinct: a COMMIT (an immutable snapshot object in the graph), a BRANCH (a movable reference — literally a tiny file in .git/refs/heads/<name> holding one commit hash), and HEAD (a pointer that normally points at a branch ref, recording which branch is "current"). Creating a branch writes one small file naming the current commit — no files are copied, which is why branching is instant even on a huge repo. When you commit, git writes the new commit object with the current commit as its parent, then advances the CURRENT branch ref to the new commit and lets HEAD follow, because HEAD points AT the branch, not directly at the commit. Switching branches repoints HEAD to another branch ref and rewrites your working tree to match that branch's snapshot. Multiple branches point into one shared object graph and only diverge where they add different commits — the common history is shared, never duplicated. (If HEAD ever points directly at a commit instead of a branch, you are in "detached HEAD" — commits you make there belong to no branch and can be lost, which is a preview of the reflog lesson.) Once you see a branch as a 41-byte pointer, "make a branch for it" stops feeling heavy and becomes the default safe move.

remotes-push-pull-fetch.proof: A local clone linked to a bare "remote" repo where you push a commit and read back the commit the remote branch now points at.
remotes-push-pull-fetch.unlock: You can explain why fetch is always safe, why pull can change your working tree, and what origin/main actually is.
remotes-push-pull-fetch.outcome: Model a remote as a named URL, distinguish fetch (download only) from pull (fetch + integrate) from push (upload), and reason about remote-tracking branches.
remotes-push-pull-fetch.doNotClaim: Don't claim pull and fetch are interchangeable — fetch never touches your branch; pull fetches AND merges/rebases into it.

remotes-push-pull-fetch.text: You run git pull to "just get the latest" and it drops you into a merge conflict mid-task, or worse, silently merges upstream work into your half-done branch. The surprise is that pull is two operations glued together, and you only wanted one of them. This lesson separates fetch from pull so "get the latest" stops being a gamble.

A REMOTE is just a named bookmark for another repository's URL (conventionally "origin"). Git keeps REMOTE-TRACKING branches like origin/main — read-only local mirrors of where the remote's branches were as of your last fetch. Three verbs move data: git fetch downloads new commits and updates origin/* but touches NONE of your local branches; git pull runs fetch and then integrates origin/<branch> into your current branch (merge by default, or rebase); git push uploads your commits and advances the remote branch. Seeing origin/main as a cached pointer is the key to predicting all three.

remotes-push-pull-fetch.prompt: Before reading: git fetch just ran and printed new commits. Did your current branch, your working tree, or origin/main change?
remotes-push-pull-fetch.reveal: Only origin/main (and other remote-tracking refs) changed — it now points at the newly downloaded commits. Your current local branch and your working tree are untouched, which is exactly why fetch is safe to run anytime. To actually incorporate those commits you would then merge or rebase origin/main into your branch (which is what pull does in one step).

remotes-push-pull-fetch.code:
git remote add origin <url>   # name the remote 'origin' (just a URL bookmark)
git fetch origin              # download new commits; update origin/* ONLY (safe)
git log --oneline main..origin/main   # commits upstream has that you don't (preview!)
git merge origin/main         # NOW integrate them into your branch (pull = fetch+this)
git push origin main          # upload your commits; advance the remote's main
remotes-push-pull-fetch.intro: Wire a remote, fetch to update the mirror, then compare your branch to origin before integrating.
steps: A remote is a named URL; origin is the conventional name for "where I cloned from".
fetch updates remote-tracking refs (origin/*) and nothing else — always non-destructive.
main..origin/main lists what upstream has that you lack — inspect before integrating.
push sends your commits up and moves the remote branch; it is rejected if you are behind.
remotes-push-pull-fetch.commonMistake: Running git pull on a dirty working tree to "sync", then being surprised by a conflict or an unwanted merge commit. Fetch first, inspect main..origin/main, and integrate on purpose — pull hides the fetch/integrate seam that you often want to control.

remotes-push-pull-fetch.text: Collaboration is pointer synchronization across repositories. A REMOTE is a named URL (origin by convention) for another copy of the repo. For each remote branch, git maintains a REMOTE-TRACKING branch locally — origin/main is a read-only pointer recording where the remote's main was the last time you fetched. It is a CACHE, not live: it only moves when you fetch. The three verbs each do one clear thing. git fetch contacts the remote, downloads any new objects, and updates the origin/* pointers — it never modifies your local branches or working tree, so it is always safe. git pull is a convenience that does fetch AND THEN integrates origin/<branch> into your current branch, using merge by default (creating a merge commit if histories diverged) or rebase if you configure pull.rebase — this is the step that can conflict or rewrite your working tree, which is why "just pulling" sometimes surprises people. git push uploads your new commits and fast-forwards the remote branch; if the remote has commits you do not (you are behind), the push is REJECTED and you must integrate first. The disciplined loop is: fetch, inspect `main..origin/main` to see what is incoming, then merge or rebase deliberately, then push. Split the operations and remote work becomes predictable instead of a slot machine.
remotes-push-pull-fetch.title: fetch downloads, pull integrates, push uploads — origin/main is a cached pointer
fetch vs pull vs push across two repos
remotes-push-pull-fetch.subtitle: origin/main is a local cache of the remote

storyboard.say: The remote repo, origin, is just another copy of your project living at a URL. It holds commits your machine hasn't seen yet.
git fetch contacts origin and downloads any new commits it finds. Nothing about your local work changes yet.
Fetch's only job is to update origin/main, a read-only cache pointer recording where the remote's main was as of this fetch.
Now comes the second, separate step: integration. You choose merge or rebase to bring those incoming commits toward your branch.
Integration rewrites your local main, and this is where conflicts erupt. git pull glues fetch plus this step together, so pull can surprise you mid-task.
Going the other direction, git push takes your local commits and sends them upward.
Push uploads your work to origin and advances the remote's branch, so teammates can fetch it next.
The insight: fetch is always safe and only moves the cache; pull secretly adds the risky integrate step. Split them and the surprise disappears.

pull-requests-review.proof: A repo where you compute the exact commit list and changed-file set that a PR from feature into main would contain.
pull-requests-review.unlock: You can produce and read the base..feature range that a PR is built from, without a web UI.
pull-requests-review.outcome: Prepare a branch that reviews well: a focused commit range on top of the base, a readable diff, and a clean base..feature comparison — the raw material a pull request wraps.
pull-requests-review.doNotClaim: Don't claim a PR is a git feature — it is a platform (GitHub/GitLab) workflow around a branch; git's part is the reviewable commit range.

pull-requests-review.text: Your pull request gets "too big to review" and sits for days. The problem is upstream of the web UI: the branch carried twelve unrelated commits and a 900-line diff. A PR is only as reviewable as the branch behind it. This lesson teaches you to shape that branch — the commit range and diff — so review is fast, using pure git so you understand what the platform is showing.

A pull request is a code-review and merge workflow provided by a hosting PLATFORM (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) — it is NOT a git command. What git contributes is the reviewable substance: the set of commits on your feature branch that are not on the base (main..feature) and the combined diff of that range. Reviewers read commit-by-commit and file-by-file, so a branch with focused commits and a tight diff reviews in minutes, while a sprawling one stalls. You can compute exactly what a PR will show — commits and changed files — locally, before you ever open it.

pull-requests-review.prompt: Before reading: which commits does a PR from feature into main display — every commit on feature, or only the ones not already on main?
pull-requests-review.reveal: Only the commits on feature that are NOT reachable from main — the range main..feature. Commits already on main are shared history and are not part of the PR. That is why keeping your branch rebased/updated on main keeps the PR showing only YOUR work, and why an out-of-date base can make a PR display confusing extra commits.

pull-requests-review.code:
git log --oneline main..feature   # the commits the PR will contain (feature minus main)
git diff --stat main..feature     # the files + line counts the PR diff will show
git diff main...feature           # 3-dot: changes on feature since it forked from main
# a good PR: few focused commits, a small --stat, one logical change
pull-requests-review.intro: Compute the PR's commit range and its changed-file set the way the platform does.
steps: main..feature (two dots) = commits reachable from feature but not from main — the PR commit list.
git diff --stat summarizes the changed files and their +/- line counts at a glance.
The 3-dot diff main...feature shows what feature added relative to the common ancestor.
A reviewable PR has a short commit range and a small, single-purpose diff.
pull-requests-review.commonMistake: Opening a PR from a branch that also contains unrelated commits (a stray refactor, a merge of main, debug commits). The range main..feature then includes noise, ballooning the diff and burying the actual change reviewers need to see.

pull-requests-review.text: A pull (or merge) request is a PLATFORM feature — a place to discuss, review, and approve a branch before it is merged into a base branch. Git itself has no "PR" object; what it provides is the reviewable content, and knowing that content is what lets you shape a good PR. The commits a PR displays are the range base..feature: commits reachable from your feature tip but NOT from the base branch — i.e., your new work, with shared history excluded. The diff a PR shows is typically the 3-dot diff base...feature, meaning "what feature changed relative to the point where it forked from base," which is stable even if base moved on. Two knobs make a branch review well. First, SCOPE: one logical change per branch, so base..feature is a handful of related commits and git diff --stat is small — reviewers can hold the whole change in their head. Second, HISTORY HYGIENE: commits with clear messages, no debug noise, and a base kept up to date (so the range shows only your commits, not accidental extras). Because you can compute both the commit list (git log base..feature) and the file set (git diff --stat base..feature) locally, you can self-review a PR before opening it — catching the "too big" and "why is that file here" problems while they are still cheap to fix.

When the scope is focused and the diff is tight, the reviewer can approve and merge your branch back into main.
The insight: a PR is only as reviewable as the branch behind it — shape the range and diff before you ever open the web UI.

resolving-merge-conflicts.proof: A repo with a deliberate conflict that you resolve to a chosen final content, then commit — printing the resolved file and clean status.
resolving-merge-conflicts.unlock: You can read <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> markers and know that staging the resolved file is what tells git the conflict is settled.
resolving-merge-conflicts.outcome: Understand why a conflict happens (both sides changed the same region), read the conflict markers, resolve by choosing the intended content, and complete the merge.
resolving-merge-conflicts.doNotClaim: Don't claim a conflict is git 'breaking' — it is git refusing to guess when two changes overlap; resolving it is a human decision git then records.

resolving-merge-conflicts.text: A merge stops with "Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit." Panic sets in, someone runs git merge --abort or force-pushes over it, and work is lost. A conflict is not an error state — it is git handing you a decision it cannot make. This lesson demystifies the markers and the resolve-stage-commit loop so conflicts become routine.

Git merges by combining two branch tips against their common ancestor (a three-way merge). Where only one side changed a region, git takes that change automatically. A CONFLICT occurs only where BOTH sides changed the SAME region differently — git cannot know which you want, so it pauses and writes both versions into the file between markers: <<<<<<< HEAD (your side), =======, >>>>>>> other (their side). Resolving means editing the file to the correct final content, removing the markers, then git add-ing it (which records the resolution in the index) and committing to complete the merge.

resolving-merge-conflicts.prompt: Before reading: two branches each changed line 10 of config.yml to different values, then you merge. What does git do?
resolving-merge-conflicts.reveal: It reports a conflict on config.yml. Because both sides changed the SAME line relative to the common ancestor, git cannot auto-pick a winner, so it writes both versions into the file surrounded by <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> markers and pauses the merge. You choose the correct final line, delete the markers, git add the file (marking it resolved), and commit to finish the merge. If they had changed DIFFERENT lines, git would merge cleanly with no conflict.

resolving-merge-conflicts.code:
git merge feature
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.yml
cat config.yml
# <<<<<<< HEAD
# timeout: 30            <- your side (current branch)
# =======
# timeout: 60            <- their side (feature)
# >>>>>>> feature
# --- edit the file to the intended final value, delete all three markers ---
git add config.yml       # staging the resolved file = "this conflict is settled"
git commit               # completes the merge with the resolution recorded
resolving-merge-conflicts.intro: Trigger a conflict, read the markers, resolve to the intended content, and finish the merge.
steps: A three-way merge auto-combines non-overlapping changes; it only pauses on overlaps.
The markers wrap BOTH versions: HEAD is your current branch, the name after >>>>>>> is the other.
You edit the file to the single correct final content and remove all conflict markers.
git add the resolved file records the resolution in the index; the commit finalizes the merge.
resolving-merge-conflicts.commonMistake: Committing a file that still contains <<<<<<< or >>>>>>> markers. git does not re-check the content once you add it, so the markers ship into the codebase and break the file. Always grep for markers before you stage the resolution.

resolving-merge-conflicts.text: Merging combines two lines of development. Git uses a THREE-WAY merge: it looks at your branch tip, the other branch tip, and their common ancestor (the merge base). For any region, if only ONE side changed it relative to the base, git takes that change automatically — most of a merge is silent and correct. A CONFLICT arises only where BOTH sides changed the SAME region in different ways: git has no basis to choose, so instead of guessing it pauses the merge and rewrites the conflicted file to contain both candidate versions, delimited by markers: everything between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is YOUR current-branch content, and everything between `=======` and `>>>>>>> <name>` is the OTHER side. The file is now in a conflicted state and the path sits in the index with multiple stages. Resolution is a human decision expressed as an edit: you change the file to the single intended final content — which might be your side, their side, a blend, or something new — and you delete all three marker lines. Then `git add <file>` collapses the index entry to your resolved version, signaling "settled." When every conflict is staged, `git commit` writes the merge commit (which has two parents). Two escape hatches exist: `git merge --abort` throws the whole merge away and returns to the pre-merge state, and `git checkout --ours/--theirs <file>` takes one side wholesale. The mental model is calm: git only asks you about genuine overlaps, and the loop is always resolve → add → commit.
resolving-merge-conflicts.title: A conflict is an overlap git refuses to guess; you resolve, stage, commit

rebase-vs-merge.proof: Two repos from the same divergence: one merged (a merge commit, two parents) and one rebased (linear, no merge commit) — proven by commit counts and parent counts.
rebase-vs-merge.unlock: You can state what each does to history and why you must never rebase commits others have based work on.
rebase-vs-merge.outcome: Choose between merge (preserve history, add a merge commit) and rebase (replay commits for a linear history, new hashes) and know the golden rule about rebasing shared commits.
rebase-vs-merge.doNotClaim: Don't claim one is universally better — merge preserves the true graph, rebase rewrites for readability; the choice depends on whether the commits are shared.

rebase-vs-merge.text: A teammate rebased a branch everyone had already pulled and force-pushed it. The next morning three people had duplicate commits and mysterious conflicts, and half a day vanished untangling it. Rebase is powerful and dangerous for exactly one reason: it rewrites history. This lesson gives you the decision rule so you get rebase's clean history without detonating your team's.

Two ways to integrate a diverged branch. MERGE creates a new merge commit with TWO parents, tying both histories together — the real graph is preserved, including the fork and join. REBASE instead REPLAYS your commits one by one on top of the target tip, producing brand-new commits with NEW hashes and a straight, linear history — the original commits are abandoned. The golden rule: never rebase commits that have been pushed and that others may have based work on, because rewriting their hashes desynchronizes everyone who has the originals.

rebase-vs-merge.prompt: Before reading: after rebasing feature onto main, are feature's commits the same objects as before? What changed?
rebase-vs-merge.reveal: No — they are NEW commit objects with different hashes. Rebase replays each original commit as a fresh commit on top of main (same changes, new parent, new hash, possibly new committer date), and the old commits are left unreferenced. That hash change is exactly why rebasing shared commits is dangerous: anyone who already has the old hashes now diverges from your rewritten ones.

rebase-vs-merge.code:
# MERGE: keep both histories, create a merge commit (two parents)
git switch main
git merge feature            # -> a new merge commit joining main and feature

# REBASE: replay feature's commits onto main for a linear history (new hashes)
git switch feature
git rebase main              # feature's commits are recreated on top of main
git switch main
git merge feature            # now a fast-forward: no merge commit, straight line
rebase-vs-merge.intro: Integrate the same divergence two ways and see the shape each produces.
steps: merge adds ONE commit with two parents; the branch/fork structure stays visible in the graph.
rebase recreates your commits atop the target — same diffs, new hashes, linear history.
After a rebase, merging into main is usually a fast-forward (just moves the pointer).
Rebase abandons the original commits; only rebase commits that are yours and unshared.
rebase-vs-merge.commonMistake: Rebasing a branch that has already been pushed and pulled by others, then force-pushing. Everyone who had the old commits now has divergent duplicates — the classic team-wrecking mistake. Rebase local, unshared work only. Two more senior gotchas: rebase replays conflicts PER commit, so a long branch can force you to resolve the same conflict again and again — turn on `git rerere` to auto-reuse past resolutions. And on most teams the real integration step is neither a raw merge nor a shared rebase but a squash-merge on the PR (one clean commit per branch), which keeps main linear without ever rewriting anyone else’s commits.

rebase-vs-merge.text: Both merge and rebase integrate a diverged branch, but they produce different HISTORY. MERGE creates a single new merge commit with TWO parents — one on each branch tip — so the true topology is preserved: you can always see that feature forked from main at some point and rejoined here. Nothing is rewritten; existing commits keep their hashes. The cost is a busier graph with merge commits. REBASE takes the opposite approach: it finds your branch's commits since the fork, and REPLAYS each one, in order, on top of the target branch's current tip. Each replayed commit is a BRAND-NEW object — same change, but a new parent and therefore a new hash (and the originals become unreferenced). The result is a clean, linear history with no merge commits, which reads like the work was done sequentially. The trade is that history is now a curated fiction rather than the literal record. This leads to the ONE rule that matters: the golden rule of rebasing — never rebase commits that have been pushed and that others may have based work on. Rewriting their hashes means anyone who already fetched the originals now has a divergent history, producing duplicate commits and confusing conflicts when they next sync, often "fixed" with a destructive force-push. So: rebase your OWN local, unpushed commits to keep a branch tidy before review; MERGE (or accept a merge) when the commits are shared. Many teams combine both — rebase your feature locally to clean it up, then merge it into main via a PR.
rebase-vs-merge.title: Merge preserves the graph; rebase rewrites it linear — never rewrite shared commits

undo-safely.proof: A repo where you unstage a file with restore --staged and revert a commit, printing the porcelain status and the post-revert file content.
undo-safely.unlock: You can name which of the three trees each undo touches and why revert is the only safe undo for pushed commits.
undo-safely.outcome: Pick the right undo for the situation: restore (discard working-tree/staged edits), reset (move a branch pointer across the three trees), or revert (a new commit that undoes a shared one).
undo-safely.doNotClaim: Don't claim 'git reset' is THE undo — reset --hard destroys uncommitted work, and reset on pushed commits rewrites shared history; the right tool depends on what you are undoing.

undo-safely.text: Someone runs git reset --hard to "undo the last thing" and wipes an hour of uncommitted work, or resets a pushed commit and breaks everyone's clone. "Undo" in git is not one button — it is three tools that touch different parts of the system. This lesson maps each undo to what it actually moves, so you never reach for the destructive one by reflex.

Recall the three trees: working tree, index, HEAD. Each undo targets different ones. git restore operates on files: it discards working-tree edits (restore <file>) or unstages (restore --staged <file>), leaving history alone. git reset moves the current BRANCH pointer to another commit, with --soft (move HEAD only), --mixed (also reset the index, the default), or --hard (also overwrite the working tree — destructive). git revert does NOT move anything backward: it creates a NEW commit whose changes cancel a previous commit, which is the only history-safe way to undo something already pushed.

undo-safely.prompt: Before reading: you staged a file by mistake but want to keep your edits. Which command, and what happens to the file's content?
undo-safely.reveal: git restore --staged <file>. It unstages the file — copies HEAD's version back into the INDEX for that path — but leaves your WORKING-TREE edits untouched. So the change is no longer staged, yet your edits are preserved on disk. (git reset <file> does the same unstage; restore --staged is the modern, clearer spelling.)

undo-safely.code:
git restore file.txt            # discard UNSTAGED edits to file.txt (working tree ← index)
git restore --staged file.txt   # unstage file.txt but KEEP edits (index ← HEAD)
git reset --soft HEAD~1         # undo last commit, KEEP changes staged (moves HEAD only)
git reset --hard HEAD~1         # undo last commit AND discard changes (destructive!)
git revert HEAD                 # NEW commit that undoes HEAD — safe for pushed history
undo-safely.intro: Three undos for three situations, each touching a different tree.
steps: restore <file> throws away unstaged working-tree edits — the file goes back to the index version.
restore --staged <file> unstages but keeps your edits; only the index entry changes.
reset moves the branch pointer: --soft keeps index+tree, --mixed resets index, --hard resets both.
revert adds a new commit that reverses an old one — nothing is rewritten, so it is safe when shared.
undo-safely.commonMistake: Using git reset --hard to undo a commit whose changes you actually wanted to keep — it discards them from BOTH the index and the working tree with no prompt. If you want to keep the work, use --soft or --mixed; --hard is for genuinely throwing changes away.

undo-safely.text: There is no single "undo" in git — there are targeted tools, and choosing right means knowing WHICH of the three trees each one moves. git RESTORE works at the file level and never touches history: `git restore <file>` overwrites the working-tree copy with the index version (discarding unstaged edits), and `git restore --staged <file>` copies HEAD's version into the index (unstaging while keeping your working-tree edits). git RESET moves the current BRANCH pointer to a target commit and then, depending on the flag, adjusts the other trees: --soft moves HEAD only (your changes remain staged), --mixed (the default) also resets the index so changes become unstaged, and --hard also overwrites the working tree — which permanently discards uncommitted work. Because reset MOVES a branch pointer, using it on commits you have already pushed rewrites shared history and is dangerous for the same reason rebase is. git REVERT is the opposite philosophy: it does not move anything backward; it computes the inverse of a commit's changes and records a brand-new commit that applies that inverse. History grows forward, every original commit stays intact, and everyone who pulls simply gets the reversing commit — which is why revert is the correct undo for anything already shared. The decision tree: discarding local file edits → restore; undoing a local, unpushed commit → reset (pick soft/mixed/hard by whether you want to keep the changes); undoing a pushed commit → revert.
undo-safely.title: Match the undo to the tree it touches; revert is the only safe undo for shared commits
Three undos across the three trees
undo-safely.subtitle: restore (files) · reset (pointer) · revert (new commit)

storyboard.say: "Undo" in git isn't one button. It starts with one question: what exactly are you trying to take back?
If you're undoing file edits — unstaged or staged — the answer is git restore, which works only on files.
Restore never touches history: it discards working-tree edits or unstages, so it's always safe on your local files.
If you're undoing a local commit, git reset moves your branch pointer back to an earlier commit.
Reset rewrites history, so use it on local commits ONLY — reset a pushed commit and you break everyone's clone.
For a commit that's already pushed and shared, use git revert instead of reset.
Revert makes a NEW commit that cancels the old one, leaving history intact — safe when others already have it.
Match the undo to where the change lives: files use restore, local commits use reset, shared commits use revert.

optionA.text: git revert makes a new commit that cancels the bad one. History only moves forward; everyone pulls the fix normally. The bad commit stays visible in history, which is honest and safe.
optionA.label: revert

optionB.text: Moves main back and discards the commit locally, then requires a force-push. Rewrites history others already have — duplicates, conflicts, and lost work follow.
optionB.label: reset --hard

undo-safely.guidance: For anything already pushed, revert (A) — it is the only undo that does not rewrite shared history. Reserve reset (B) for local, unpushed commits. The tell: if others might have the commit, you revert, you do not reset.

options: git restore HEAD — pulls files back to the HEAD version, dropping the last commit edits from the tree.
git reset --hard HEAD~1 — moves HEAD back one commit and also discards that commit changes from disk entirely.
git reset --soft HEAD~1 — moves HEAD back one commit but leaves that commit changes staged to recommit.
