reflog-recovering-work.proof: A repo where you commit, hard-reset to drop it, then recover the exact content by finding the commit in the reflog and resetting back to it.
reflog-recovering-work.unlock: You can explain why a "lost" commit still exists (it is unreferenced, not deleted) and how the reflog gives you its hash back.
reflog-recovering-work.outcome: Use the reflog — git's local log of where HEAD and branches have pointed — to recover commits after a bad reset, a deleted branch, or a botched rebase.
reflog-recovering-work.doNotClaim: Don't claim reset --hard permanently deletes a commit — it becomes unreferenced but lives until garbage collection, and the reflog remembers its hash.

reflog-recovering-work.text: Panic: a git reset --hard or an aborted rebase just "deleted" a commit with an hour of work. People assume it is gone and redo it from memory. It is almost never gone — git keeps a private log of every position HEAD has held, and the reflog turns that panic into a two-command recovery. This lesson is the safety net that makes every other destructive command survivable.

Every time a ref (HEAD or a branch) moves — commit, checkout, reset, merge, rebase — git appends an entry to that ref's REFLOG, recording the old and new commit and what moved it. Entries are addressable as HEAD@{0}, HEAD@{1}, and so on. Crucially, when reset --hard or a deleted branch "drops" a commit, the commit OBJECT still exists in the database (it is merely unreferenced); the reflog still holds its hash, so you can point a ref back at it and the work returns. The reflog is LOCAL and expires (reachable entries after 90 days, unreachable after 30 by default), but that window is enormous for recovery.

reflog-recovering-work.prompt: Before reading: you run git reset --hard HEAD~1 and realize the dropped commit had work you need. Is it gone, and how would you get it back?
reflog-recovering-work.reveal: It is not gone — reset --hard only moved the branch pointer; the commit object is still in the database, just unreferenced. Its hash is recorded in the reflog (HEAD@{1} is where HEAD was before the reset). You recover with `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` (or find the hash via `git reflog` and reset/checkout to it). The work returns exactly as it was.

reflog-recovering-work.code:
git reflog                      # every position HEAD has held, newest first:
                                # abc1234 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
                                # def5678 HEAD@{1}: commit: the work I "lost"
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}       # move the branch back to where it was pre-reset
# or grab the hash and re-point precisely:
git reset --hard def5678        # def5678 is the "lost" commit from the reflog
reflog-recovering-work.intro: Read the reflog and point a branch back at a commit a reset dropped.
steps: Every ref movement (commit, reset, checkout, rebase) appends a reflog entry with the old→new hash.
HEAD@{N} names where HEAD was N moves ago — HEAD@{1} is "just before the last move".
A reset --hard only repoints the branch; the dropped commit object still exists, unreferenced.
Point a ref back at the reflog entry (or the raw hash) and the commit is referenced again — recovered.
reflog-recovering-work.commonMistake: Assuming the reflog is shared or permanent. It is LOCAL to your clone (a teammate's reflog cannot recover YOUR lost commit) and entries expire (default 90/30 days), so recover promptly and do not rely on it as a substitute for pushing or committing.

reflog-recovering-work.text: The reflog is git's local, per-ref history of POINTER movements — distinct from commit history, which records project snapshots. Every time HEAD or a branch ref changes (a commit, checkout, reset, merge, rebase, or pull), git appends an entry to that ref's reflog capturing the previous hash, the new hash, and the operation. You address entries with the `ref@{N}` syntax: HEAD@{0} is the current position, HEAD@{1} is where HEAD was one move ago, and `main@{2}` is where main was two moves ago. Why this is a lifesaver: git objects are IMMUTABLE and are not deleted the instant a ref stops pointing at them. When reset --hard, a deleted branch, or an aborted rebase "loses" a commit, that commit object still sits in the database — it is merely UNREFERENCED (no ref or reachable ancestor points to it). The reflog still holds its hash, so recovery is just pointing a ref back at it: `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` or `git checkout -b rescue <hash>`. Unreferenced objects are only actually removed by garbage collection, and even that respects the reflog expiry windows — reachable entries default to gc.reflogExpire = 90 days and unreachable ones to gc.reflogExpireUnreachable = 30 days. Two caveats keep you honest: the reflog is LOCAL (it exists only in your clone; it cannot recover a commit you never had), and it expires — so it is a recovery net, not a backup. Held together with the previous lesson: reset feels dangerous, but the reflog is why it is survivable.
reflog-recovering-work.title: The reflog remembers every ref position, so unreferenced commits are recoverable
Recovering a commit dropped by reset --hard
reflog-recovering-work.subtitle: the object survives; the reflog holds its hash

You read the reflog, find HEAD@{1}, and recover the exact hash git said it forgot.

stash-cherry-pick.proof: A repo where you stash a dirty change, verify a clean tree, restore it with pop, then cherry-pick one commit onto another branch and print the applied content.
stash-cherry-pick.unlock: You can explain when stash beats a throwaway commit, and how cherry-pick copies a diff rather than moving a branch.
stash-cherry-pick.outcome: Shelve uncommitted work with stash to switch context safely, and copy a single commit's change onto another branch with cherry-pick.
stash-cherry-pick.doNotClaim: Don't claim stash 'saves' work like a commit — it is a temporary local stack that is easy to lose; it is a shelf, not a save.

stash-cherry-pick.text: You are mid-change when an urgent hotfix must go out on another branch. Committing half-done work pollutes history; losing it is worse. Separately, one good commit lives on the wrong branch and you need just that change over here. Stash and cherry-pick are the two precision tools for these exact situations. This lesson makes both concrete so context-switching stops costing you work.

git STASH records your uncommitted working-tree and index changes onto a local stack and reverts the working tree to HEAD, giving you a clean slate to switch branches or pull. `git stash pop` re-applies the top entry and drops it; `git stash apply` re-applies but keeps it on the stack. git CHERRY-PICK takes an EXISTING commit and applies its change as a NEW commit on your current branch — it copies the diff, it does not move the branch or its history. Both can conflict (same resolve-add-continue loop as a merge). Stash is for "hold this, I'll be right back"; cherry-pick is for "I want that one change here."

stash-cherry-pick.prompt: Before reading: you have uncommitted edits and must urgently switch to another branch to fix something. What is the clean way to set your work aside and get it back?
stash-cherry-pick.reveal: git stash — it saves your uncommitted changes onto a stack and restores the working tree to a clean HEAD, so you can switch branches freely. After the hotfix, come back and git stash pop re-applies your changes and removes them from the stack. This avoids both a half-baked "wip" commit and the risk of carrying dirty changes across a switch.

stash-cherry-pick.code:
git stash                 # shelve uncommitted changes; working tree back to clean HEAD
git switch hotfix         # now safe to switch — tree is clean
# ...fix the hotfix, commit...
git switch feature
git stash pop             # re-apply the shelved changes and drop them from the stack

# copy ONE commit from another branch onto this one:
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d   # applies that commit's diff as a NEW commit here
stash-cherry-pick.intro: Shelve dirty work, switch, then restore it — and separately copy one commit across branches.
steps: stash pushes your working-tree + index changes onto a stack and cleans the working tree.
pop re-applies the top stash and removes it; apply re-applies but leaves it on the stack.
cherry-pick takes one existing commit and re-applies its diff as a new commit on HEAD.
The cherry-picked commit is a NEW object (new hash) — the original stays on its branch.
stash-cherry-pick.commonMistake: Treating git stash as durable storage and piling up many stashes, then losing track. Stashes are unnamed by default, local, and easy to drop or forget — use them for brief context switches, not as a parking lot for work you should have committed to a branch.

stash-cherry-pick.text: These are two different recovery/mobility tools that people often confuse. git STASH addresses uncommitted work. It takes the changes in your working tree and index, records them as stash entries on a LOCAL stack, and resets the working tree to match HEAD — giving you a clean state without making a commit. You retrieve them with `git stash pop` (apply the top entry and remove it from the stack) or `git stash apply` (apply but keep it, so you can apply the same changes to multiple branches). It is a shelf: temporary, local, unnamed unless you use `git stash push -m`, and therefore not a substitute for committing important work. git CHERRY-PICK addresses commits, not working-tree changes. Given the hash of an EXISTING commit anywhere in the graph, it computes that commit's diff (versus its parent) and applies it to your current branch as a BRAND-NEW commit with a new hash — the original commit stays exactly where it was. This is how you pull a single bug-fix commit from a feature branch onto a release branch without merging the whole branch. Both operations replay changes, so both can hit CONFLICTS, resolved with the same edit → git add → continue loop you learned for merges. Rule of thumb: reach for stash when you need to PAUSE and come back; reach for cherry-pick when you want ONE specific change moved to where you are now.
stash-cherry-pick.title: Stash shelves uncommitted changes; cherry-pick copies one commit's diff

storyboard.say: You're mid-change with a dirty working tree when an urgent hotfix must ship on another branch. You can't commit half-done work.
git stash shelves your uncommitted working-tree and index changes onto a local stack, no commit made.
With changes shelved, git resets the tree to HEAD, giving you a clean slate to switch branches and fix the hotfix.
When you're back, git stash pop restores the top entry and drops it from the stack.
Your edits land back in the working tree, exactly where you left off — the shelf was temporary and local.
Cherry-pick solves a different problem: one good commit already lives on the wrong branch.
git cherry-pick copies that commit's diff and applies it as a NEW commit on your current branch.
Insight: stash pauses-and-resumes uncommitted work; cherry-pick copies an existing commit's diff — two tools people confuse.

git init -q; git config user.email a@b.c; git config user.name Dev; git symbolic-ref HEAD refs/heads/main

echo "unfinished edit" >> notes.txt        # dirty working tree
git stash >/dev/null

git stash pop >/dev/null
echo "after pop last line: $(tail -n 1 notes.txt)"
# now build a commit on a side branch and cherry-pick it onto main:

git add <resolved-files>

stash-cherry-pick.symptom: After git stash pop you get a conflict, and you are unsure whether the stash was consumed, leaving you afraid to retry.

optionB.label: wip commit

For work you want to survive a machine loss or share, a wip commit (B) you later squash is safer, because a stash is local and easy to lose. Match the tool to how long and how important the pause is.

git-bisect.proof: A repo with a bug introduced at a known commit where bisect run identifies that commit automatically, and you print its subject.
git-bisect.unlock: You can explain why bisect needs O(log n) tests instead of O(n), and what the good/bad labels and exit codes mean.
git-bisect.outcome: Locate the exact commit that introduced a bug by binary search between a known-good and known-bad commit, manually and with git bisect run.
git-bisect.doNotClaim: Don't claim you 'found the bug' by reading commits one by one — bisect is a binary search; for 1000 commits it is ~10 tests, not 1000.

git-bisect.text: A test that passed last release now fails, and there are 800 commits in between. Checking them one by one is a day of work. git bisect turns that into about ten checks by binary-searching the history: it repeatedly halves the range until the single breaking commit is cornered. This lesson teaches the algorithm and its automation so "when did this break" becomes a ten-minute answer.

Commits form an ordered history, so if a behavior was GOOD at commit A and BAD at commit B, the first bad commit is somewhere between — and you can binary-search for it. git bisect start; git bisect good <A>; git bisect bad <B> tells git the boundaries; git then checks out the MIDPOINT and asks you to test it. You answer git bisect good or git bisect bad, and git halves the remaining range each time — O(log n) steps. `git bisect run <cmd>` automates the loop entirely, using the command's EXIT STATUS (0 = good, 1–127 except 125 = bad, 125 = skip/untestable) to decide each step. bisect reset returns you to where you started.

git-bisect.prompt: Before reading: a bug is somewhere in 1024 commits between a good and a bad point. Roughly how many commits must you TEST with a binary search to pinpoint it?
git-bisect.reveal: About 10 — because each test halves the remaining range (1024 → 512 → 256 → ... → 1), and log2(1024) = 10. A linear scan could take up to 1024 tests; bisect's binary search collapses that to ~log2(n). That exponential reduction is the entire reason bisect exists and why it scales to huge histories.

git-bisect.code:
git bisect start
git bisect bad                 # current commit is broken
git bisect good v1.4           # this old tag was known good
# git checks out the midpoint; you test it, then answer good/bad:
git bisect good                # this midpoint works -> bug is newer
# ...repeat; git narrows to one commit...
git bisect reset               # done: return to your original checkout

# fully automated: git runs your test at each step and reads the EXIT CODE
git bisect start HEAD v1.4
git bisect run ./run-tests.sh  # exit 0 = good, 1..127 (not 125) = bad, 125 = skip
git-bisect.intro: Drive a bisect manually, then automate it with a test command and exit codes.
steps: You give bisect one BAD and one GOOD commit to bound the search range.
git checks out the midpoint; you test and label it good or bad, halving the range each time.
After ~log2(n) steps git reports the FIRST bad commit — the one that introduced the bug.
git bisect run <cmd> automates it via exit status: 0 good, 1–127 (≠125) bad, 125 skip.
git-bisect.commonMistake: Labeling the boundaries backwards — marking the OLD commit bad and the NEW one good. bisect assumes the transition goes good→bad forward in time; swap them and it searches the wrong half and fingers the wrong commit. The current broken commit is bad; a past working one is good.

git-bisect.text: git bisect finds the commit that introduced a regression by BINARY SEARCH over the commit history. The premise: there is a point in time where the behavior was GOOD and a later point where it is BAD, and commits are ordered, so the "first bad commit" is a boundary you can search for. You seed the search with two labels — a known-bad commit (often HEAD) and a known-good commit (an old tag or release) — which defines a range. git then checks out the COMMIT IN THE MIDDLE of that range and asks you the single question: is this one good or bad? Your answer eliminates HALF the remaining commits: if the midpoint is good, the bug is newer (search the upper half); if bad, the bug is at or before it (search the lower half). Repeat, and the range halves every step, so a history of n commits is pinpointed in about log2(n) tests — ~10 for 1000 commits, ~20 for a million. That logarithmic cost is the whole value. Manually you answer `git bisect good`/`git bisect bad` each round; to AUTOMATE, `git bisect run <cmd>` runs a test command at each checkout and interprets its EXIT STATUS: 0 means good, 1–127 (except the special 125) means bad, and 125 means "untestable, skip this commit." When the search converges, git names the first bad commit; `git bisect reset` restores your original HEAD. bisect turns "somewhere in hundreds of commits" into a short, mechanical hunt — and combined with a scripted test, into a fully hands-off one.
git-bisect.title: Bisect binary-searches history: O(log n) tests to the first bad commit
Binary search for the first bad commit
git-bisect.subtitle: each test halves the range

storyboard.say: A test that passed at release v1.4 now fails at HEAD, with 800 commits in between to blame.
You seed the search with two boundaries: a known-good commit as the lower bound and a known-bad one as the upper.
Git checks out the exact midpoint of that range and asks the single question: is this commit good or bad?
Your answer eliminates half the commits: good moves the lower bound up, bad moves the upper bound down.
The halved range becomes the new search window, and git tests its midpoint again, over and over.
You can automate every answer: git bisect run executes a test script and reads its exit code.
After about ten checks the range shrinks to one, cornering the exact commit that introduced the regression.

git-bisect.check: first bad commit subject: commit 4 breaks it
git-bisect.title: Automatically find the breaking commit
git-bisect.starter:
git init -q; git config user.email a@b.c; git config user.name Dev; git symbolic-ref HEAD refs/heads/main
# Build history: each commit APPENDS a distinct line so every commit changes content.
# The app "works" until commit 4, which introduces a FAIL on the last line.
for i in 1 2 3; do echo "step $i PASS" >> log.txt; git add log.txt; git commit -qm "commit $i works"; done
echo "step 4 FAIL" >> log.txt; git add log.txt; git commit -qm "commit 4 breaks it"
for i in 5 6; do echo "step $i FAIL" >> log.txt; git add log.txt; git commit -qm "commit $i still broken"; done
# A test: exit 0 (good) if the last line has no FAIL, non-zero (bad) if it does.
printf '#!/bin/sh\ntail -n 1 log.txt | grep -qv FAIL\n' > test.sh; chmod +x test.sh

#   git bisect bad HEAD >/dev/null 2>&1
#   OUT=$(git bisect good "$GOOD" 2>/dev/null; git bisect run ./test.sh 2>/dev/null)
#   git bisect reset >/dev/null 2>&1

#   echo "first bad commit subject: $(git log -1 --pretty=%s "$BADHASH")"
git-bisect.summary: Build a history where a specific commit breaks a test, then let git bisect run find it via exit codes and print the culprit's subject. git performs the binary search and identifies the commit — you do not tell it the answer.

git-bisect.fix:
git bisect reset
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD        # the current, broken commit is BAD
git bisect good v1.0       # the old, working commit is GOOD
git-bisect.task: The good/bad labels are reversed, so bisect searches the wrong direction. Correct the labels.
git-bisect.symptom: git bisect run reports the WRONG commit as the culprit — one that is clearly fine.
git-bisect.brokenCode:
git bisect start

gitignore-hooks.proof: A repo with a .gitignore that ignores a build dir and a .env but keeps a needed file via negation — proven by git status --porcelain showing only what should be tracked.
gitignore-hooks.unlock: You can predict which files a set of .gitignore patterns will hide, and explain why an already-tracked file keeps showing up.
gitignore-hooks.outcome: Keep junk and secrets out of a repo with .gitignore patterns (anchoring, directory, negation) and understand that ignore only affects UNTRACKED files; know what a git hook is.
gitignore-hooks.doNotClaim: Don't claim .gitignore removes a committed file — ignore rules apply only to UNTRACKED files; a tracked file must be git rm --cached to stop tracking.

gitignore-hooks.text: A repo ships node_modules, a 200MB build folder, and — worst — a committed .env with real credentials. Someone "added .gitignore" but the files kept getting committed, because the files were already tracked. .gitignore is precise but has one rule people miss. This lesson makes ignore patterns predictable so secrets and junk stay out for good.

A .gitignore file lists patterns for files git should leave UNTRACKED (never suggest adding). The patterns have real grammar: a bare name like build matches anywhere; a trailing slash build/ matches directories only; a leading slash /build anchors to the .gitignore's directory; a leading ! NEGATES (re-includes) a previously ignored pattern; and * / ? / [] are globs. The one rule that trips everyone: ignore ONLY affects untracked files — if a file is already tracked, .gitignore does nothing until you untrack it with git rm --cached. Separately, HOOKS are scripts in .git/hooks that git runs at lifecycle events (e.g. pre-commit) to enforce policy locally.

gitignore-hooks.prompt: Before reading: you add `.env` to .gitignore, but git keeps trying to commit changes to it. Why, and how do you fix it?
gitignore-hooks.reveal: Because .env was already TRACKED (committed at least once) before you ignored it — .gitignore only affects UNTRACKED files, so it does nothing to a file git already tracks. Fix: stop tracking it with `git rm --cached .env` (which removes it from the index but keeps it on disk) and commit; now the .gitignore rule takes effect and git ignores it going forward. (And rotate the leaked secret.)

gitignore-hooks.code:
cat > .gitignore <<'EOF'
node_modules/        # trailing slash: ignore this directory anywhere
/dist                # leading slash: anchored to repo root only
*.log                # glob: every .log file
.env                 # the secret — must NOT be committed
!.env.example        # negation: but DO keep the example template
EOF
git rm --cached .env         # already tracked? untrack it so the ignore takes effect
git status --porcelain       # confirm .env is gone and node_modules/dist are hidden
gitignore-hooks.intro: Write patterns that ignore a directory and a secret, keep one file via negation, and untrack an already-committed file.
steps: A trailing slash (node_modules/) matches directories; a leading slash (/dist) anchors to root.
*.log is a glob matching every log file at any depth.
!.env.example re-includes a file that a broader pattern would have ignored.
ignore affects only UNTRACKED files; git rm --cached untracks an already-committed one.
gitignore-hooks.commonMistake: Adding a secret or a huge file to .gitignore AFTER it was already committed and assuming it is now safe. The file is still tracked (and still in history); you must git rm --cached it to stop tracking, and the secret in past commits still needs rotating.

gitignore-hooks.text: A .gitignore is a list of PATTERNS describing files git should treat as intentionally untracked — it keeps them out of git status's "untracked" noise and prevents `git add .` from staging them. The pattern grammar is worth knowing precisely: a plain string (build, secret.key) matches that name at ANY directory depth; a trailing slash (logs/) restricts the match to DIRECTORIES; a leading slash (/dist) ANCHORS the pattern to the directory containing the .gitignore (usually the repo root) so it does not match nested dist/ folders; standard globs apply (* any run of non-slash characters, ? one character, [abc] a set); and a leading ! NEGATES an earlier pattern, re-including a file that would otherwise be ignored (order matters — a negation must come after the rule it overrides). The single most important rule, and the source of nearly every "why won't it ignore my file" question: .gitignore only affects UNTRACKED files. Once a file is tracked (committed at least once), git keeps tracking it regardless of .gitignore; to actually stop, you run `git rm --cached <file>` to remove it from the index (leaving it on disk) and commit that. This is why a leaked .env cannot be "un-leaked" by ignoring it — it is tracked and, worse, already in history. HOOKS are the other pro tool: executable scripts under .git/hooks (pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push, and more) that git invokes at those lifecycle moments; a non-zero exit from pre-commit aborts the commit, which teams use to run linters, block secrets, or enforce message formats locally. Hooks are local and not committed by default, so they are shared via tooling, not the repo itself.

tags-releases.proof: A repo where you create both a lightweight and an annotated tag and print each tag's object TYPE, proving annotated tags are real objects.
tags-releases.unlock: You can explain why a tag is a stable pointer (unlike a branch) and when to prefer annotated tags.
tags-releases.outcome: Mark releases with tags, choosing annotated tags (a real object with metadata) over lightweight ones, and understand tags as fixed pointers that do not move.
tags-releases.doNotClaim: Don't claim a tag and a branch are interchangeable — a branch moves as you commit; a tag stays pinned to one commit, which is the entire point for releases.

tags-releases.text: A hotfix must go out for "the version we shipped Tuesday," but there is no marker — just a branch that has moved on twenty commits since. Without tags, "which commit was v2.1.0" is archaeology. Tags pin a name to an exact commit forever. This lesson makes releases addressable so you can always check out, diff, or fix the precise version you shipped.

A TAG names a specific commit permanently. Two kinds exist. A LIGHTWEIGHT tag is just a ref pointing at a commit — a bookmark, nothing more. An ANNOTATED tag (created with -a) is a full tag OBJECT stored in the database: it records the tagger's name, email, and date, a message, and can be GPG-signed — and it points at the commit. Unlike a branch, a tag does NOT advance when you commit; it stays fixed, which is exactly what a release marker needs. Convention is semantic versioning (vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, e.g. v2.1.0). Annotated tags are recommended for releases precisely because they carry who/when/why.

tags-releases.prompt: Before reading: what is the difference between tagging a commit and creating a branch at it?
tags-releases.reveal: A branch is a MOVABLE pointer — commit while on it and it advances. A tag is a FIXED pointer — it stays on the exact commit you tagged no matter what you commit next. That immovability is why tags mark releases: v2.1.0 must always mean the same commit, forever, so you can return to it. A branch called "v2.1.0" would drift the moment someone committed on it.

tags-releases.code:
git tag v1.0.0-light                     # lightweight: just a ref to the commit
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First stable release"   # annotated: a real object with metadata
git cat-file -t v1.0.0                    # -> tag   (an annotated tag is an OBJECT)
git cat-file -t v1.0.0-light              # -> commit (lightweight = points straight at commit)
git show v1.0.0                           # shows tagger, date, message, then the commit
git tag                                   # list all tags
tags-releases.intro: Create a lightweight and an annotated tag and see that only the annotated one is a real object.
steps: A lightweight tag is a bare ref to a commit — cat-file resolves it straight to a commit.
An annotated tag (-a) creates a tag OBJECT storing tagger, date, and message.
cat-file -t proves the difference: the annotated tag's own type is "tag", not "commit".
A tag never moves as you commit — it stays pinned to the release commit.
tags-releases.commonMistake: Using lightweight tags for releases. They carry no tagger, date, or message, so you lose the audit trail of who cut the release and when — annotated tags exist for exactly this, and they can be signed for authenticity.

tags-releases.text: Where a branch is a MOVABLE pointer that follows your commits, a TAG is a FIXED pointer that stays on one specific commit — permanently. That immovability is the whole reason tags mark releases: the name v2.1.0 must resolve to the same commit forever so you can check it out, diff against it, or branch a hotfix from it long after main has moved on. There are two flavors, and the difference is real. A LIGHTWEIGHT tag is simply a reference (a file under .git/refs/tags/) that points directly at a commit — a private bookmark with no extra data. An ANNOTATED tag, created with `git tag -a <name> -m <msg>`, creates an actual TAG OBJECT in the database: it stores the tagger's name and email, the date, a message, and optionally a GPG signature, and it in turn points at the commit. You can prove the distinction with `git cat-file -t`: an annotated tag's own object type is "tag," while a lightweight tag resolves straight to "commit." Because annotated tags carry who/when/why and can be verified with a signature, they are the recommended choice for releases — the lightweight kind is fine for a quick private marker. The near-universal naming convention is SEMANTIC VERSIONING: vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where a MAJOR bump signals breaking changes, MINOR adds backward-compatible features, and PATCH is backward-compatible fixes. Tags are not pushed automatically — `git push --tags` (or pushing a specific tag) shares them — which is a deliberate design so your local markers stay local until you choose to publish a release.
tags-releases.title: A tag is a fixed pointer; annotated tags are real objects with release metadata
Lightweight vs annotated tags on the release commit
tags-releases.subtitle: a tag pins a name; annotated adds a metadata object

An annotated tag goes further: the name v1.0.0 names a real tag object stored in the database, not just a bare ref.
That tag object records the tagger's name, email, date, and message, can be GPG-signed, and points at the same commit.
Both flavors pin one commit forever, and unlike a branch a tag never moves when you commit again.
So v1.0.0 always resolves to the same commit: you can check it out, diff it, or branch a hotfix long after main moved on.

terminal-power-user.proof: A script whose && / || chain runs a command only on success and a fallback only on failure, printing which branch executed based on real exit codes.
terminal-power-user.unlock: You can predict whether the right side of && or || runs from the left side's exit status, and write a safe compound command.
terminal-power-user.outcome: Chain commands by exit status with && and ||, sequence with ;, and define git aliases — turning multi-step workflows into single, exit-code-aware lines.
terminal-power-user.doNotClaim: Don't claim ; and && are the same — ; runs the next command regardless, && runs it only if the previous SUCCEEDED; using ; where you needed && is how broken pipelines march on.

terminal-power-user.text: A deploy script runs `build; upload` and happily uploads a BROKEN build because ; ignores the build's failure. Meanwhile you retype the same long git commands fifty times a day. Two power-user habits fix both: chaining on exit status (&&/||) so failures stop the line, and aliases so common commands are two letters. This lesson turns the shell from a launcher into a controller.

Every command returns an EXIT STATUS: 0 means success, non-zero means failure. The shell operators branch on it. `A ; B` runs B unconditionally after A. `A && B` runs B ONLY if A succeeded (exit 0). `A || B` runs B ONLY if A failed (non-zero). Combined, `A && B || C` runs B on success and C on failure. Jobs let you background long tasks (cmd & to background, jobs to list, fg to foreground). git ALIASES (git config alias.co checkout) shorten frequent commands. These small tools compound into fast, safe, repeatable workflows.

terminal-power-user.prompt: Before reading: `make build && ./deploy.sh` — what happens to deploy if the build fails? What if you had used a semicolon instead?
terminal-power-user.reveal: With &&, deploy.sh runs ONLY if make build succeeded (exit 0); a failed build (non-zero) short-circuits and deploy never runs — which is what you want. With a semicolon (make build ; ./deploy.sh), deploy.sh runs regardless, so a broken build gets deployed. && is the guard that makes a chain stop on failure.

terminal-power-user.code:
make build && ./deploy.sh          # deploy ONLY if the build succeeds (exit 0)
git pull || echo "pull failed"     # run the fallback ONLY if pull fails (non-zero)
lint && test && ship               # each step gates the next; any failure stops the line
git config alias.st "status -sb"   # now 'git st' == 'git status -sb'
git config alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --decorate"   # 'git lg' for a compact graph
terminal-power-user.intro: Guard steps with exit-status operators and define an alias for a frequent command.
steps: Exit status 0 = success, non-zero = failure; the operators branch on it.
&& runs the right side only on success; || runs it only on failure.
Chaining lint && test && ship stops at the first failing step — a broken build never ships.
git config alias.X turns a long command into a short one you actually remember.
terminal-power-user.commonMistake: Sequencing critical steps with ; instead of &&. `test ; deploy` deploys even when tests fail, because ; ignores exit status. Use && to make each step depend on the previous one succeeding.

terminal-power-user.text: The unifying idea of shell control flow is the EXIT STATUS: every command finishes with a numeric code, 0 for success and non-zero for failure, and the shell operators read it. `A ; B` is plain sequencing — B runs after A no matter what A returned. `A && B` is conditional-AND — B runs ONLY if A exited 0; if A failed, the shell SHORT-CIRCUITS and skips B. `A || B` is conditional-OR — B runs ONLY if A exited non-zero, making it the natural "fallback on failure." These compose: `deploy && notify_success || notify_failure` notifies success after a good deploy and failure otherwise (with the caveat that || binds to the whole left side). This is why a safe pipeline is `lint && test && build && ship` — the first failing stage stops the line, so nothing broken proceeds; swapping in semicolons silently marches past failures. JOB CONTROL handles long-running work: append `&` to run a command in the background, `jobs` lists background jobs, `fg`/`bg` move them between foreground and background, and Ctrl-Z suspends the current one. Finally, ALIASES eliminate repetition: `git config alias.co checkout` (or shell `alias gs="git status"`) turns commands you type dozens of times a day into a couple of keystrokes, and a git alias starting with `!` can even run a shell command. Together these turn the terminal from a place you launch one command at a time into a place you express exit-code-aware, repeatable workflows in a single line.
terminal-power-user.title: Exit status drives && / ||; aliases compress the commands you repeat
Branching on exit status with && and ||
terminal-power-user.subtitle: success gates the next step; failure triggers the fallback

storyboard.say: Every command you run leaves behind an exit status, and command A is where our story starts.

If A failed with a non-zero code, the double-pipe path fires instead, running fallback C.
Because success gates the next step, a passing B lets the chain flow onward to the next command.
That's why a safe pipeline reads lint && test && ship: any failure short-circuits and stops the line.

capstone-recover-and-ship.text: A repo is in a bad state: main has a commit that broke the app, and a good change is stranded. Your job is the full professional loop — figure out what happened with log/diff, recover or isolate the good work onto a clean feature branch, produce a reviewable PR range (only your commits), verify the fix, and tag the release. This capstone wires every module into one deliverable.

Real git work is never one command — it is a COMPOSITION. This capstone chains the course: Module 1's shell fluency to script it, Module 2's history reading to diagnose, Module 3's branch/PR-range thinking to isolate the fix, Module 4's recovery (reset/revert/reflog) to undo the bad change safely, and Module 5's tags to mark the release. The output is what a teammate would review: a clean base..feature range containing only the intended commits, a verified fix, and an annotated release tag — the same artifact every prior lesson pointed toward.

capstone-recover-and-ship.prompt: Before reading: main has a commit that broke the build, and it has already been shared. What is your ordered plan to fix and ship — which tools, in what order?
capstone-recover-and-ship.reveal: A reasonable order: (1) INSPECT with git log/diff to identify the bad commit and confirm what it changed; (2) because it is SHARED, undo it with git revert (not reset) to avoid rewriting history; (3) branch the real fix with git switch -c so main stays clean and the PR is scoped; (4) commit the fix and VERIFY the range with git log base..feature and git diff; (5) tag the release with an annotated tag. Inspect → revert → branch → fix → verify → tag.

capstone-recover-and-ship.code:
git log --oneline -n 5                       # 1. inspect: find the bad commit
git show HEAD                                 # confirm what it changed
git revert --no-edit HEAD                     # 2. undo safely (shared history) — new commit
git reflog --format='%H %gs'                  # 3. find the STRANDED good commit's hash
git switch -c fix/restore-config <hash>       #    recover it onto a clean branch (reflog is the net)
git log --oneline main..fix/restore-config    # 4. verify: only your commits in the range
git tag -a v1.0.1 -m "restore config, harden build"   # 5. tag the release
capstone-recover-and-ship.intro: The end-to-end loop: diagnose, undo safely, recover stranded work from the reflog, isolate on a branch, verify the range, tag.
steps: Inspect with log/diff/show to identify and confirm the breaking commit.
Undo it with revert (history is shared), producing a forward-only fix commit.
Recover the stranded good commit from the reflog — its hash survives even after the branch that held it is deleted.
Isolate that recovered work on a scoped branch so main stays clean and the PR is tidy, then verify the range shows only your commit.
Tag the release with an annotated tag once the range is clean.
capstone-recover-and-ship.commonMistake: Fixing directly on main with a reset/force-push instead of revert+branch. On shared history that rewrites everyone's clones; the professional loop reverts forward and isolates the fix on a branch that becomes a reviewable PR.

capstone-recover-and-ship.text: This capstone is not a new command — it is the JUDGMENT to sequence the whole course into a real recovery-and-ship workflow, choosing the safe tool at each step. The loop, and why each choice is right: (1) INSPECT — git log --oneline, git show, and git diff tell you what actually happened before you touch anything; never operate blind on a broken repo. (2) UNDO SAFELY — if the bad commit is already shared, git revert records a NEW commit that cancels it, keeping history forward-only; you use reset only for local, unpushed mistakes, and the reflog is your net if a recovery goes sideways. (3) ISOLATE — put the real fix on a scoped feature branch (git switch -c) so main stays a known-good pointer and the change becomes a reviewable unit; this is the branch-as-cheap-pointer idea paying off. (4) VERIFY THE RANGE — git log base..feature and git diff --stat confirm the PR contains ONLY your intended commits and files, so review is fast and nothing stray ships; this is the PR-range discipline from Module 3. (5) TAG — an annotated tag marks the exact shipped commit with who/when/why, so the release is addressable forever and future bisects have a good boundary. Underneath it all is Module 1's shell fluency (you can script and chain these steps with && so a failure stops the line) and Module 2's object model (every step is really moving or adding pointers and commits in the graph). The mark of a git professional is not knowing revert or bisect in isolation — it is composing them, with the right safety choice at each fork, into a clean, provable outcome.

The recover-and-ship loop end to end

storyboard.say: The loop opens where every recovery must: inspect. Log, show, and diff tell you what actually broke before you touch anything.
Once you've identified the bad commit, you undo it. Because it's already shared, revert records a new canceling commit and keeps history forward-only.
Now fix forward: isolate the real work on a scoped feature branch with switch -c, so main stays a known-good point.
Commit the fix on that branch, then verify the whole range so only your clean commits ship as a reviewable base..feature diff.
This is the decision gate: only when the range is clean do you move on. A dirty range sends you back to inspect, never forward.
Range clean, so mark the release with an annotated tag — a durable, signed pointer to this known-good state.
Ship: the output is a clean PR a teammate can review. The capstone was never one command — it's the judgment to sequence the safe tool at each step.

capstone-recover-and-ship.title: Recover, fix, verify, and tag — end to end
capstone-recover-and-ship.starter:
git init -q; git config user.email a@b.c; git config user.name Dev; git symbolic-ref HEAD refs/heads/main
# --- given: main has a build-breaking commit, AND a good change was stranded ---
echo "config: valid" > config.txt; git add config.txt; git commit -qm "working config"
# the good change was committed on a scratch branch, then the branch was DELETED —
# so that commit is now stranded (reachable only through the reflog):
git switch -c scratch 2>/dev/null
echo "config: valid+hardened" > config.txt; git add config.txt; git commit -qm "harden config validation"
git switch main 2>/dev/null
git branch -D scratch >/dev/null
# meanwhile main took a commit that broke the build:
echo "config: BROKEN" > config.txt; git add config.txt; git commit -qm "oops broke config"

# 1. inspect what is on main now
echo "bad commit was: $(git log -1 --pretty=%s)"
# 2. undo the bad commit SAFELY — main is shared, so revert forward (never reset)
git revert --no-edit HEAD >/dev/null
echo "after revert config: $(cat config.txt)"
# 3. recover the stranded good commit from the reflog onto a clean rescue/PR branch
lost=$(git reflog --format='%H %gs' | grep 'harden config validation' | head -1 | awk '{print $1}')
git switch -c fix/harden-config "$lost" 2>/dev/null
echo "recovered stranded work: $(cat config.txt)"
echo "reflog rescue hash matches: $([ "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" = "$lost" ] && echo yes || echo no)"
# 4. verify the PR range shows ONLY the rescued commit
echo "PR range commits:"; git log --pretty=format:'%s' main..fix/harden-config && echo
# 5. tag the release (annotated). TODO: create the tag, then print it + its object type:
#   git tag -a v1.0.1 -m "restore + harden config"
#   echo "release tag: $(git tag) (type $(git cat-file -t v1.0.1))"
capstone-recover-and-ship.summary: A repo where main has a build-breaking commit AND a good change was stranded when its branch was deleted. Run the full professional loop: inspect, revert the breakage safely on shared main, recover the stranded commit from the reflog onto a clean branch, verify the PR range shows only that commit, then tag the release. Every reported fact is computed by git across the whole loop.

capstone-recover-and-ship.fix:
git fetch origin                            # see the damaged remote — do NOT reset --hard to it
git reflog show origin/main                 # find the good tip from BEFORE the force-push
git reset --hard <good-tip>                 # restore local main to the pre-push commit
                                            #   (reset --hard DISCARDS uncommitted work — stash first if any)
git push --force-with-lease origin main     # publish the restore, after telling the team to pause pushes
# only NOW, if a commit genuinely broke the build, undo it FORWARD (never reset shared history again):
git revert <bad-commit>
git switch -c fix/whatever                  # isolate any follow-up fix as a reviewable PR
capstone-recover-and-ship.task: The force-push rewrote shared history. Recover the good pre-push tip from the reflog and restore it — do NOT reset your local main to the damaged remote, and never rewrite shared history to fix it.
capstone-recover-and-ship.symptom: A teammate "fixed" a broken shared main by running git reset --hard HEAD~1 and git push --force. That force-push dropped a commit everyone else still has; now their pulls are rejected and the pre-push tip of main looks lost.
capstone-recover-and-ship.brokenCode:
git reset --hard HEAD~1   # rewrote shared history
git push --force          # broke everyone's clone; no PR, no review

optionA.text: Revert the bad commit forward, isolate the real fix on a branch, open a reviewable PR, then tag. History stays intact, teammates just pull, and the change is reviewed before merge.
optionA.label: Revert + branch + PR

optionB.text: Move main back and force-push the fix. Fewer steps, but it rewrites shared history (breaking clones) and skips review entirely — the exact failure this course warns against.
optionB.label: Reset + force-push

capstone-recover-and-ship.guidance: Always A on shared history. The professional loop — inspect, revert forward, isolate, verify, tag — is safe, reviewable, and auditable. B (reset + force-push on shared history) is the anti-pattern the recovery and rebase lessons exist to prevent.
capstone-recover-and-ship.question: To ship the fix for a broken shared main, revert-and-branch for a PR, or reset-and-force-push directly?

options: Inspect with log/diff, revert the bad commit forward, isolate the fix on a branch, verify the range, then tag the release.
Reset --hard back one commit and force-push over main, since rewriting the shared branch is the fastest way to erase it.
Delete the local repository and re-clone from origin, then push the fix, treating a fresh clone as the safe reset.
Commit the fix straight onto main with no branch, review, or tag, because a broken build is urgent enough to skip process.

capstone-recover-and-ship.explanation: On shared history you undo with revert (forward-only), isolate the fix on a scoped branch for a reviewable PR, verify the range contains only your commits, and tag the release. Resetting and force-pushing shared history (option 1) rewrites everyone's clones and skips review — the anti-pattern.
